Article Title: In 2021, researchers began placing concrete-block oyster reefs in bare eelgrass patches on Prince Edward Island; within two years biomass was about 45 times higher and 45 taxa had colonised the struct
Article Text:
Representative Image (AI-generated)

Turning bare seabed into new habitat

Life quickly began to gather

Fish began using the reefs too

The reefs are not a replacement for eelgrass

Connecting restoration with the local community

What happens next

What started as piles of concrete blocks on the seafloor off Prince Edward Island soon became a magnet for marine life. Researchers began installing the artificial oyster reefs in 2021 to test whether they could provide some of the ecological functions lost from areas where eelgrass no longer grew. Within two years, the structures had been colonised by 45 taxa, while biomass was about 45 times higher on two-year-old reefs than on newly installed ones. The findings, published in Ecosphere , show how a simple structure can provide a new foothold for marine life in a fragmented coastal habitat.The work took place on the eastern end of Lennox Island, Prince Edward Island, where eelgrass (Zostera marina) meadows are broken up by patches of bare sediment. Instead of trying to plant eelgrass directly into those empty areas, researchers tested another idea. They built small artificial reefs from ordinary concrete blocks and placed them in the bare patches.The first 18 reefs went into the water in July 2021. Another 16 were added in 2022, followed by eight more in 2023. Each reef was made from eight to 10 concrete blocks arranged into a mound, creating several levels and surfaces above the seabed.The blocks gave oysters and other organisms something that bare sediment could not: a hard surface to settle on and grow. That was important because oyster reefs are more than collections of oysters. As they develop, they can create three-dimensional habitat that other marine organisms can use for shelter, feeding and attachment.The structures did not remain bare for long. Researchers recorded 45 taxa across 11 phyla on the artificial reefs. They included plants, invertebrates and fish, with 29 of the taxa identified to species level. Oyster spat, or newly settled oysters, were among the first organisms to establish themselves. As the reefs aged, the community became more developed. The difference in biomass was particularly striking. Reefs that were less than a year old had an average biomass of about 35 grams. That increased to roughly 318 grams on one-year-old reefs.By the time the reefs were two years old, average biomass had reached about 1,577 grams. That was around five times the biomass recorded on one-year-old reefs and roughly 45 times the amount found on the newly installed structures. Much of that increase came from oysters growing on the reefs. The number of different taxa also changed as the structures matured. One-year-old reefs had an average of about 19 taxa, compared with roughly seven on the newest reefs.The structures were not simply places for oysters and other organisms to attach themselves. Researchers also observed fish using the older reefs for feeding and shelter. Fish diversity and evenness generally increased with reef age, although the fish observations were analysed descriptively because sample sizes were limited. Measurements also showed differences in several water-quality conditions around the reefs compared with nearby bare areas. Compared with nearby bare areas, the reef sites had lower temperatures and turbidity, higher dissolved oxygen and lower pH in the measurements recorded by the researchers. In other words, the reefs were beginning to affect their surroundings as well as provide a physical surface for marine life. That matters because one of the problems with fragmented coastal habitats is that losing a habitat-forming species can affect many other organisms that depend on it. Creating another type of structure may help fill at least some of that gap.The researchers do not suggest that concrete oyster reefs can simply replace eelgrass meadows. The project explored whether artificial reefs could provide some of the ecological functions of eelgrass habitat in areas where eelgrass was already absent. That distinction is important. Restoring eelgrass can be difficult when the environmental conditions responsible for its decline have not changed. Simply planting more eelgrass may not solve the underlying problem.An oyster reef offers a different approach. Rather than recreating the lost habitat exactly, it introduces another type of habitat that can support marine life under the existing conditions. The researchers describe this as ecological facilitation, with different habitat-forming species potentially providing complementary benefits.The project was carried out in collaboration with the Lennox Island First Nation. The researchers note that oyster beds have historical ecological, cultural and food-security importance in the area and that many have since disappeared.The artificial reefs therefore offered a way to create new habitat while also supporting the return of oysters and other organisms. The researchers recorded species including lobster and forage fish using the developing structures. The approach is relatively simple, too. Concrete blocks are inexpensive, readily available and can be placed using a small boat, making the method potentially useful for smaller restoration projects.The results are encouraging, but the researchers point out that the reefs will need to be watched for longer to understand how their communities develop and how they interact with nearby eelgrass. A two-year-old reef is still relatively young, and the ecological effects could change as oysters continue to grow and more organisms arrive. Still, the experiment offers an interesting lesson in habitat restoration. Sometimes restoring a damaged ecosystem may not mean trying to recreate exactly what was there before. In fragmented coastal areas, creating new structures that give marine life somewhere to settle, feed and shelter could provide another way to rebuild some of the functions that have been lost.On Prince Edward Island, a collection of concrete blocks has already become a small but growing marine community, showing how quickly life can make use of a new piece of habitat.
Article Summary: Oyster reefs were built from concrete blocks on Prince Edward Island. Within two years, the structures had been colonised by 45 taxa. biomass was about 45 times higher on two-year-old reefs than on newly installed ones. The reefs are not a replacement for eelgrass but a way to support marine life.

Article Title: A 1950 Washington bridge carrying about 90,000 vehicles a day is getting a $114 million overhaul; engineers will replace its movable span with a fixed one floated into place during a single 56-hour cl
Article Text:
As per the report, engineers will use accelerated bridge construction methods to limit disruption to one of the region's busiest transportation corridors.

A major rebuild for a 1950 bridge

New span floated into position

Heavy construction activity through 2029

A bridge that has carried Washington traffic for more than seven decades is headed for a major transformation, but commuters may barely notice the most dramatic part of the work. The nearly half-mile-long Northbound I-395 bridge over the Potomac River is set for a $114 million rehabilitation that will replace its movable span with a new fixed structure during one tightly scheduled 56-hour weekend closure, states an online report by Field News. The construction is expected to begin next year, with completion planned for fall 2029, adds the report.According to Field News, Skanska USA Civil will lead the design-build project for the District Department of Transportation, working with AECOM and Genesis Structures on the design team. The project is jointly funded by DDOT and the Federal Highway Administration. Built in 1950, the four-lane bridge carries roughly 90,000 vehicles every day and forms part of a five-structure crossing connecting Arlington, Virginia, with Washington, D.C. , adds the report.The rehabilitation will go well beyond repairing an aging roadway. One of its central elements is the replacement of the existing 175-foot, double-leaf bascule span, the movable section that allows river traffic to pass.As per the report, engineers will use accelerated bridge construction methods to limit disruption to one of the region's busiest transportation corridors. Instead of constructing the replacement span entirely in place, the new fixed section will be assembled beside the existing bridge.It will then be floated into position during a single 56-hour weekend closure, the report explains.Also, the compressed installation window is expected to require specialised marine equipment, rigging and carefully coordinated construction crews. The project will also replace the vessel protection system around the bascule piers and upgrade bridge barriers to meet modern collision standards. Approach spans will undergo superstructure and substructure rehabilitation, while overhead sign structures, lighting and drainage systems affected by construction will also be replaced, adds the report.The bridge sits beside Skanska's separate Long Bridge North project, a roughly $1 billion effort being delivered with FlatironDragados to expand rail capacity through the same Arlington-Washington corridor. With both projects progressing in the same area, the river crossing zone is expected to remain a significant centre of heavy civil construction through the end of the decade.For contractors and subcontractors, the I-395 rehabilitation is expected to create opportunities across several specialised areas, including marine work, structural steel, traffic control, signage, lighting, drainage and bridge-barrier upgrades. The most unusual phase will be the float-in operation, where decades of bridge history will give way to a new fixed span in less than three days.Image Courtesy: ARL Now
Article Summary: The Northbound I-395 bridge over the Potomac River is set for a $114 million rehabilitation that will replace its movable span with a new fixed structure. The construction is expected to begin next year, with completion planned for fall 2029. The four-lane bridge carries roughly 90,000 vehicles every day.

Article Title: Trump-Xi summit: $14 billion Taiwan arms deal hangs over Washington talks
Article Text:
File photo: US president Donald Trump with Chinese premier XI Jinping

$14 billion Taiwan deal remains on hold

Beijing wants arms deliveries stopped

Xi could ‘lecture’ Trump on Taiwan

Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected to press US President Donald Trump to halt arms sales to Taiwan when the two leaders meet in Washington this week. Sources have informed Reuters that Beijing is likely to invoke a 1982 US-China agreement that commits Washington to gradually reducing weapons sales to Taipei.The issue is likely to be among the most sensitive points in Xi’s talks with Trump, as Beijing considers Taiwan a core sovereignty issue and has repeatedly demanded an end to US arms sales to the self-governed island.Three sources briefed on US-China discussions told Reuters that Beijing is expected to raise its interpretation of the third of the three US-China joint communiques, signed in 1982.Under the communique, Washington said it intended to gradually reduce its arms sales to Taiwan and did not seek to maintain long-term weapons sales to Taipei.But an accompanying memo by then-US President Ronald Reagan said the US commitment to reduce arms sales was “conditioned absolutely” on China’s continued commitment to resolving differences with Taiwan peacefully.The distinction is significant because China has sharply expanded its military activity around Taiwan in recent years, including military exercises involving live missile tests. Chinese forces now operate around the island on an almost daily basis, according to Reuters.The Trump administration approved an $11 billion arms package for Taiwan in December, described as the largest such package to date. But a second package worth about $14 billion has remained on hold for months.Trump said after meeting Xi in Beijing in May that he was keeping the package in abeyance and described it as a “very good negotiating chip”.A White House official said Trump would decide on the new package within a relatively short period.Trump approved more arms sales to Taiwan during his first term than any previous US president, the official said, adding that his second-term approvals in the first year had already exceeded the total approved during all four years of Joe Biden’s presidency.Taiwan’s foreign ministry said it was closely monitoring the US-China exchanges while maintaining communication with Washington.China is also seeking an end to deliveries of weapons that Taiwan has already ordered from the US, according to the sources, who spoke on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the discussions.One source said Xi could tell Trump that Taiwan was the “provocateur” and the source of instability in US-China relations, while accusing Taipei of changing the status quo.Beijing could offer cooperation in putting pressure on Iran over the Middle East war in return, the sources said.China’s foreign ministry has said Washington must honour the three joint communiques and previous commitments on Taiwan, calling this a necessary condition for stable and healthy US-China ties.The US, however, maintains a “one China” policy under which it does not take a formal position on Taiwan’s sovereignty and acknowledges, without endorsing, Beijing’s position that Taiwan is part of China.Washington is also required by US law to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself, despite the absence of formal diplomatic relations between the US and Taipei.The 1982 agreement is not the only document shaping the US position on Taiwan.The “Six Assurances” issued to Taiwan that year, but declassified only in 2020, stated that Washington had not agreed to set a date for ending arms sales to Taiwan or to consult Beijing before approving such sales.US lawmakers have also urged Trump not to weaken Washington’s support for Taipei ahead of his meeting with Xi.Republican senator Pete Ricketts, who chairs the Senate foreign relations subcommittee on East Asia, said last week that Trump should make clear that US policy on Taiwan had not changed.John Moolenaar, the Republican chairman of the House Select Committee on China, separately told Trump that Chinese objections to US arms sales and security cooperation with Taiwan and other Asian allies should be rejected.Matt Pottinger, who served as deputy national security adviser during Trump’s first administration, said he did not expect a substantive change on Taiwan during the summit.But he predicted Xi would likely “lecture” Trump at length on Taiwan, as he had done in previous meetings with US presidents.
Article Summary: Beijing is likely to invoke a 1982 US-China agreement that commits Washington to gradually reducing weapons sales to Taipei. Issue likely to be among the most sensitive points in Xi’s talks with Trump. Beijing considers Taiwan a core sovereignty issue and has repeatedly demanded an end to US arms sales.

Article Title: A four-bedroom waterfront home was completed in California in 2026; within months, the Belvedere property is listed for $32 million; the newly built estate comes with sweeping bay views and luxury ame
Article Text:
Pic credit: Zillow

What the buyer gets

Pic credit: Zillow

Pic credit: Zillow

Pic credit: Zillow

Pic credit: Zillow

Pic credit: Zillow

A market in motion

Pic credit: Zillow

Pic credit: Zillow

Less than a year after completion, the newly built mansion at 46 Cliff Road in Belvedere hit the market. The waterfront mansion is asking $32 million, the San Francisco Business Times reported. The three-storey home sprawls across 5,000 square feet with four bedrooms, five bathrooms, and what may be its most prized perk: direct access from street to water, which is rare on Belvedere Island. The current owners, who acquired the property this year, are putting it back on the market as they are building a larger residence elsewhere.It is one of the very few places in the world where land, water, and land conspire to create something magnificent. Most homes on the island either face the water or back onto the street. This one does both. So the buyer really gets unobstructed views across the bay towards San Francisco and the Golden Gate Bridge!Set at the water's edge, this mansion has a magnificent view of the San Francisco skyline, the Golden Gate Bridge, the Marin Headlands, Sausalito, and Mount Tamalpais. The house comes with four bedrooms and five full bathrooms. The primary suite includes a walk-in wardrobe. The kitchen is clean and functional: stone counters, a gas cooktop, wine refrigerator, dishwasher, range hood, and the standard ensemble of appliances that make a modern kitchen feel complete. Wood and stone flooring flows through the main living areas, anchoring the open layout without the visual weight of wall-to-wall carpet.The living room opens onto a terrace where the bay views actually land. A fireplace and deck access make the space feel like somewhere people might actually spend time. There is a spa with a built-in hot tub outdoors and a grill, along with multiple terraces that appeal to buyers who are great hosts. The modern construction includes a two-car garage, contemporary amenities throughout, and the kind of finish that commands this price tag before the first occupant moves in.The lot itself carries history. It was last sold in May 2019 for $2.1 million before any development. The transformation from vacant land to turnkey luxury home in roughly seven years reflects the velocity of wealth appreciation in this enclave. Belvedere Island's geography, surrounded by water, with limited buildable land, creates scarcity, which keeps prices climbing.Tania Toubba, the agent listing the property through Sotheby's International Realty, told the outlet that the newly built home's owners intended to live there long-term, but they ultimately “decided they need more space and are currently building a larger home.” Quinta Properties LLC, a local family-owned builder linked to Rudolph Koppl, owns the property, the outlet reported.The $32 million listing arrives amid a flurry of activity on the peninsula. Last month, 125 Belvedere Avenue was sold for $16.9 million, sidestepping an auction through Concierge Auctions. Down the road, a nearly 10,000-square-foot property at 20 Crest Road is asking $50 million, which would set a residential record for Marin County if the sale closes at that figure.The market really started moving upwards after Apple design chief Jony Ive completed a surprise $73 million acquisition in September 2025. Ive bought four homes on the peninsula in a single off-market deal: three consecutive houses on Golden Gate Avenue and another on Beach Road. Ive's largest property, with five bedrooms, 11 bathrooms and four fireplaces, was sold for $43.5 million. This move assured Belvedere's ultra-luxury tier and appeared to catalyse price increases across the island almost immediately.Agents were flooded with calls after Ive's purchase became public. One estate down the hill from his compound bumped its asking price 10% within days. For a property in Belvedere, a 10% jump means adding millions without changing a brick.
Article Summary: Newly built mansion at 46 Cliff Road in Belvedere hit the market for $32 million. The three-storey home sprawls across 5,000 square feet with four bedrooms, five bathrooms, and direct access from street to water. Current owners, who acquired the property this year, are putting it back on the market as they are building a larger residence elsewhere.

Article Title: Meet Caymus Maxson, the 16-year-old California teen who started Trash Turtles at 10, led 50+ beach cleanups, removed 6+ tons of debris, recycled 75,000+ cigarette butts and became a 2026 Barron Prize
Article Text:
Maxson said the decision to start Trash Turtles came from seeing rubbish being pushed towards the sea (Photo: Surfrider)

,

Small action becomes youth movement

More than six tons of debris removed

Focus on plastic waste

Moving to California

At 10, Caymus 'CO' Maxson noticed something wrong on a beach in Madeira Beach, Florida. In February 2020, she saw beach trash being raked towards the water’s edge. She realised that the incoming tide could carry the waste into the sea and decided to act.Maxson soon started Trash Turtles, a youth-focused environmental nonprofit with the mission to 'Save the planet one piece of trash at a time'. Over the next six years, the organisation grew from a small effort on one beach into a network involved in beach cleanups, youth leadership and environmental campaigns.According to Surfrider FoundationTrash Turtles has now hosted more than 50 beach cleanups and removed more than six tons of trash and marine debris. It has also cleaned more than 300 miles of beaches and collected more than 75,000 cigarette butts, which were recycled through TerraCycle. The organisation has also raised $8,000 to fund three water refill stations at local schools.Maxson’s work has now received national recognition. She was named among the 2026 winners of the Gloria Barron Prize for Young Heroes, which recognises young people aged 8 to 18 for making a positive impact on people and the planet.The 2026 winners include young people working in areas such as environmental protection, technology, education and community service.Maxson said the decision to start Trash Turtles came from seeing rubbish being pushed towards the sea. “I saw a problem with trash being raked to the water’s edge, where I knew the incoming tide could carry it out to sea, and I wanted to do something about it. That moment became the start of Trash Turtles,” Maxson said as qouted by Surfrider Foundation.The organisation’s approach is based on the idea that environmental action does not always require a large campaign or a complicated solution. It can begin with a small action, such as picking up a piece of rubbish.This idea also became the #LeaveWith3 movement. It encourages people to pick up and properly dispose of at least three extra pieces of trash wherever they are, including at school, work or the beach.“#LeaveWith3 was my way of taking a big problem and creating a simple solution that everyone could understand and participate in. The idea is that if each person picks up just three pieces of trash wherever they go, together we can leave the environment a little better than we found it,” Maxson said.The numbers behind Trash Turtles show how small actions have grown over time. The organisation says it has removed more than six tons of trash and marine debris and cleaned more than 300 miles of beaches.It has also collected and recycled more than 75,000 cigarette butts through TerraCycle. Cigarette butts are among the waste items targeted by the organisation as it works to reduce pollution around coastal areas.Trash Turtles has also raised $8,000 to fund three water refill stations at local schools. The project aims to reduce reliance on single-use plastic bottles. The organisation has awarded $8,500 through its Hope Scholarship programme to eight young people.“What started with picking up trash on one beach has become so much more than I ever imagined. It showed me that one small idea can grow into something that reaches people far beyond where it started,” Maxson said.Beach cleanups are only one part of Trash Turtles’ work. Its Straw Change Campaign focuses on single-use plastic waste, including discarded plastic straws and packaging associated with products such as Capri Sun.The organisation’s approach involves identifying an environmental problem, documenting it, educating people about it and asking for change. Its work therefore goes beyond simply removing waste from beaches.Trash Turtles also focuses on helping young people understand that they can participate in solving environmental problems in their own communities.Maxson has been involved with Jane Goodall’s Roots & Shoots USA and is serving her second term on the National Roots & Shoots Youth Council. She also took part in youth leadership activities, including the 2024 Hope in Action Summit at Tropicana Field.“Young people can bring a different perspective, and our voices can make a real difference,” Maxson says.Trash Turtles has developed partnerships and collaborations with organisations including the Jane Goodall Institute’s Roots & Shoots USA, Clearwater Marine Aquarium, Tampa Bay Watch, Keep Pinellas Beautiful, Surfing’s Evolution, Preservation Foundation and Phillps. It has also worked with sustainable brands.Maxson has also worked on environmental storytelling and media projects. Along the way, she has met and collaborated with people including Dr Jane Goodall, Ian Somerhalder and Caulin Donaldson of Trash Caulin.The organisation has now moved its headquarters from Florida to Pacific Grove, California, bringing its youth-focused approach to ocean conservation to Monterey Bay.“I have come to understand that environmental issues usually stem from a normalization of everyday systems that have never been challenged,” Maxson said. “That realization makes me hopeful, because it means that change is only one choice away,” she said.Trash Turtles joined Surfrider Monterey for California Coastal Cleanup Day on Saturday at Sand City.
Article Summary: Caymus 'CO' Maxson started Trash Turtles in February 2020. It is a youth-focused environmental nonprofit with the mission to 'Save the planet one piece of trash at a time' The organisation has hosted more than 50 beach cleanups and removed more than six tons of trash and marine debris. It has also cleaned more than 300 miles of beaches and collected more than 75,000 cigarette butts.

Article Title: In 2020, Tasmania treated invasive rice grass in Duck Bay; three years later, fish species had more than doubled from 5 to 11 and average catches rose from about 2 to 45 per net
Article Text:
Among the species benefiting from the restoration are yellow-eye mullet.

How rice grass spread across wetland

Rice grass was treated with herbicide using quadbikes, vehicles with long hoses and drones. (Photo: ABC)

Native saltmarsh plants return

Fish return after rice grass removal

A major effort to remove invasive rice grass from Tasmania’s Duck Bay is showing major signs of recovery, with native vegetation returning and the number of fish species rising from five to 11. The changes came within just two to three years of the weed being removed from parts of the wetland.The restoration work is being carried out by Circular Head Landcare, which has spent almost 15 years trying to eradicate rice grass from Tasmania’s largest coastal wetlands, according to ABC news. The group, with support from farmers, has reduced the weed from about 50 hectares to just five hectares.Scientists from Univrersity of Tasmania studying the wetland also found that fish were not only returning but were using the restored saltmarsh areas for feeding. Among the species benefiting are yellow-eye mullet, which are caught both commercially and recreationally, and hardyheads, a small bait fish eaten by larger species.The restoration has required a large effort on land and in the water. Rice grass has been treated with the herbicide Fusilade Forte using quadbikes, vehicles with long hoses and, more recently, drones. Volunteers also search the coastline for seedlings that may have been missed or have grown again.Rice grass was first planted in the 1940s to beautify Smithton’s Duck River. Over the years, it spread across mudflats and saltmarsh along a 120-kilometre stretch from Woolnorth to Stanley.The weed can form dense growth that takes over areas used by native plants and animals. Sue Jennings, a volunteer with Circular Head Landcare, says the grass became increasingly dense when left untreated."All of these little sheltered bays were full of rice grass, which is a bright green, wavy grass up to your knee. It just gets thicker and thicker," Jennings said.Duck Bay is part of Tasmania’s largest coastal wetland system, which includes sheltered bays, estuaries and tidal islands. The area is also important for shorebirds, with thousands visiting Tasmania’s far north-west during summer.Some of these birds travel long distances to reach the wetland. They include the far eastern curlew, ruddy turnstone and red-necked stint. The small red-necked stint weighs only about 30 to 35 grams.Shorebird ecologist Eric Woehler says red-necked stints can travel enormous distances during their lives. "Over 20 years, red-necked stints would fly half a million kilometres, which is farther than the distance between the earth and the moon," Woehler said.The wetland also supports fish including gobies, sardines, flounder, galaxiids, garfish, leatherjackets and Australian salmon.Removing rice grass has allowed native saltmarsh vegetation to recover. Jennings says the herbicide being used kills pasture grass and rice grass but does not kill the saltmarsh plants."It kills pasture grass and it kills rice grass, but it doesn't kill the salt marsh plants. So as we get rid of the rice grass, the salt marsh plants start to recover on their own," she says.The restoration is also important for nearby oyster farms. During mass herbicide spraying, harvesting is stopped for an additional seven days as a safety measure.According to Tasmanian Oyster Company chair Jon Poke, the pause can mean a significant financial loss for the business. The company can harvest up to 18,000 to 20,000 dozen oysters a week, meaning the two-week suspension could represent a lost opportunity of nearly half a million dollars in sales.However, Poke says protecting the wetland was important for the long-term survival of the farms. "We looked at what had happened in other estuaries, and for my own business to survive, we needed to make sure that the environment was looked after. Eventually rice grass would have closed our farms down," he says.University of Tasmania scientists have been tracking changes in native saltmarsh vegetation and fish communities as the restoration continues. Wetland ecologist Vishnu Prahalad says the recovery had happened faster than expected in some areas. "After two years, three years, you wouldn't even be able to say there was rice grass there, so all the native vegetation has come back," Prahalad said.The number of fish species recorded in the restored areas increased from five to 11. Scientists also saw a major change in the number of fish caught during their surveys. In the first year, researchers struggled to find fish, catching only two across four nets. "The first year, I think we caught two fish; we struggled to look for them, and there they were, two fish across four nets, which is very unusual," Prahalad says.The difference became much clearer after the rice grass was removed. Researchers found about 200 mullets in one net. "After the rice grass was removed, in one net we had about 200 mullets," Prahalad says.Scientists then examined whether the fish were simply able to enter the area more easily or were actually using the restored habitat. They found that the fish were feeding there and eating the typical food found in a saltmarsh. "Nature bouncing back is a wonderful thing to see," says Prahlad.Circular Head Landcare hopes to finish treating the remaining rice grass meadows within the next two years, depending on weather and funding. Once the eradication work is complete, the area will be monitored for another decade. The amount of herbicide used is also expected to reduce as the weed becomes less common and the focus shifts to finding any remaining plants.
Article Summary: Rice grass was first planted in the 1940s to beautify Smithton’s Duck River. Over the years, it spread across mudflats and saltmarsh along a 120-kilometre stretch from Woolnorth to Stanley. The weed can form dense growth that takes over areas used by native plants and animals.

Article Title: UK backs Saudi Arabia with RAF Voyager refuelling support amid Houthi campaign
Article Text:
File photo: Andy Burnham

UK links support to energy security

Britain stops short of direct strikes

The UK has stated that it will provide Saudi Arabia with defensive military support, including air-to-air refuelling for Saudi fighter jets, as Riyadh faces a renewed campaign of attacks by Iran-backed Houthi forces in Yemen.Prime minister Andy Burnham said Saudi Arabia had requested military support and that Britain had agreed to provide an RAF Voyager aircraft to refuel Saudi jets for several weeks.The aircraft is expected to operate from RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus. British officials described the deployment as “time limited” and said it was intended to help Saudi Arabia defend its energy infrastructure and keep key oil routes open.The move comes as the Houthis have advanced along Yemen’s Red Sea coast and taken control of the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, a major maritime route connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden.Burnham said the decision was partly driven by concerns over the impact of the conflict on energy supplies and the cost of living in Britain.“I go back to the point I made about cost-of-living pressures and acting to secure the interests of Britain and the wider region,” Burnham told reporters from BBC.Saudi Arabia has faced a series of Houthi attacks in recent days, including missile and drone strikes targeting Riyadh and energy infrastructure along the Red Sea coast.The attacks have raised concerns over further disruption to Saudi oil exports.The UK already provides air-defence support to Saudi Arabia, including the deployment of the Sky Sabre system. The new refuelling mission will allow Saudi aircraft to remain airborne for longer while responding to incoming threats.The deployment is significantly more limited than Britain's previous military action against the Houthis.In January 2024, the UK joined the US in carrying out airstrikes against Houthi military targets in Yemen after the group attacked commercial shipping in the Red Sea. Further British-American strikes followed later that year.This time, the UK has framed its involvement as defensive support rather than direct attacks on Houthi positions.The announcement also comes as Burnham prepares for his first face-to-face meeting with US President Donald Trump at the UN. Burnham said he would urge Trump to work towards ending the war in Iran, arguing that the conflict and the wider instability in the Middle East were contributing to economic pressure in Britain.The UK government is also concerned about the wider consequences of the fighting for global energy and shipping routes. The Bab al-Mandab Strait has become a new flashpoint after the Houthis' recent advances along Yemen's Red Sea coast, while shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains severely disrupted.Burnham said Britain wanted to see the conflict end as quickly as possible and was ready to work with its allies to reduce the wider instability.
Article Summary: UK to provide air-to-air refuelling for Saudi fighter jets. Move comes as Riyadh faces renewed campaign of attacks by Iran-backed Houthi forces in Yemen. Decision driven by concerns over impact of conflict on energy supplies and cost of living.

Article Title: A 67-year-old Idaho teacher retired and drove across the US to Delaware after her daughter's daycare bill matched the mortgage; she now provides about 30 hours of childcare every week for her granddau
Article Text:
Mary Jo Galusha now spends about 30 hours each week caring for her granddaughter (NPR photo)

Rising costs push families to grandparents

Millions of grandparents provide regular care

Sacrifice for grandparents

Galusha plans to care until kindergarten

A 67-year-old retired schoolteacher from Idaho moved across the US to Delaware after her daughter decided to have a second child despite the high cost of childcare. Mary Jo Galusha retired from teaching and drove cross-country in her red Volkswagen Beetle to help her daughter, Stacia Bourne, and her family, WTJX NewsFeed reported.Bourne, a University of Delaware psychology professor who lives in Maryland, and her husband had been worried about the cost of raising another child. Their first child, George, was born in 2020 and started daycare at the age of two. "The cost for childcare for him is about the same as our mortgage," Bourne said.The couple had been discussing whether they could afford a second child when Galusha offered to help. She told her daughter that if they decided to have another baby, she would retire and move from Idaho to the East Coast to provide childcare.Several months later, Galusha received the call that Bourne was expecting. "I got a call that Stacia was expecting and that I better start planning on retiring," Galusha recalled with a laugh. She then retired from her job as a schoolteacher, packed her belongings and made the long drive to Delaware.Galusha, who is now the grandmother of five, lives in Newark, Delaware. Her granddaughter Robin was born in late 2024 and spends about 30 hours a week in Galusha's care while her parents work.Galusha has also replaced her Volkswagen Beetle with an SUV so that two car seats can fit more easily in the back row. "It's a joy," Galusha said. "It's like magic to watch them grow up."Galusha's decision comes as more families in the US are relying on grandparents for childcare. Grandparents have always helped look after grandchildren, but rising childcare costs have made that support more important for families who cannot easily afford daycare.According to Child Care Aware of America, the average annual cost of childcare for children under five in the US was $13,184 in 2025. In some cases, childcare costs can be close to the cost of rent or college tuition.Nicole Jorwic, chief programme officer at Caring Across Generations, said families are turning to older relatives because of gaps in the childcare system."The reality is that because this country hasn't invested in a childcare infrastructure that is flexible and affordable and reliable, grandparents are filling in the gaps that the service system leaves behind," she said.Madonna Harrington Meyer, a Syracuse University sociology professor who studies ageing and grandparenting, said several factors have increased the need for childcare. More households now have both parents working full-time, while the number of single mothers has also increased over the decades.Families raising children with disabilities can face another challenge because they may need childcare providers who can offer specialised care. "All of these things are reasons people turn to grandparents," Harrington Meyer said.Galusha is one of millions of grandparents who help care for grandchildren. One poll found that nearly half of respondents with grandchildren under 18 looked after them at least once every few months.An AARP report from June found that the main reasons grandparents provide childcare include parents being busy or working and grandparents wanting to spend time with their grandchildren.The median amount of time grandparents spent caring for grandchildren, excluding those who are primary caregivers or provide no care, was 200 hours a year, or about 3.8 hours a week, according to the data.Having grandparents provide childcare can also offer greater flexibility than formal daycare. Harrington Meyer said grandparents may care for children at their own homes or at the children's homes and can adjust arrangements around the family's needs."They are so flexible," Harrington Meyer said. "Unlike a formal daycare situation, often grandparents will come to your house, or they'll alternate between watching the children at their own house and at the grandparent's house."Grandparents can also benefit from spending time with their grandchildren. One study found higher scores on memory and verbal fluency tests among grandparents who provided care.However, providing regular childcare can be demanding, particularly for older people who have already raised their own children. It can affect their physical health, social lives and careers. Grandparents who move to be closer to their grandchildren may also leave behind friends and familiar surroundings.Jerry Larkin, 66, a former machinist, moved in with his daughter's family in Tulsa, Oklahoma, during the Covid-19 pandemic to help care for his twin grandsons. One of the children requires additional medical care."Being raised in the '60s, there were a lot of stay-at-home moms and everything, so this wasn't really a thing," Larkin said. "But now that everybody's got to work two jobs, it's become a thing."Yalanda Lattimore, 59, also provides regular care for her one-year-old granddaughter, Mavee. She looks after her for one and a half days each week. Lattimore said the arrangement has reduced the time she can spend on her handmade soap business and media work."I felt like I could make the sacrifice more than they could, and it truly has been a sacrifice," she said. "You just put things on hold, because your priorities are different."For Galusha, her pension from her years as a schoolteacher in Idaho makes it possible to provide unpaid childcare after retirement. Her home in Newark has a bedroom for her grandchildren, a playroom filled with Legos and a crafting area for George.Galusha and Bourne use a shared Google Calendar to organise the children's care. The current plan is for Galusha to look after Robin until she starts kindergarten, although the two review the arrangement every six months.Bourne said having her mother provide the care gives the family a sense of security, but there is little backup if the arrangement changes."I'd much prefer to have my mom take care of Robin, but then you always worry, like if in six months she decides that she wants to move and be near another grandbaby, then we'll have to scramble and figure out something else," Bourne said. Galusha responded from across the table, "No plans for that."For Lattimore, the time spent caring for her granddaughter is also about being present for her family. "What you really want is somebody to say you were there, that you were there for them," she said. "Those are the memories that I want."She said parents should not have to choose between paying for childcare and giving up work. After raising four children herself, she wanted her daughter to have a different experience."When my daughter got ready to start her family, I just didn't want her to go through that," Lattimore said. "I wanted her to have the balance. If work-life balance exists for somebody, I wanted it for my daughter," she added. For families like Bourne’s, that support can mean more than saving on childcare; it can also give grandparents a meaningful role in the everyday lives of the next generation.
Article Summary: Mary Jo Galusha, 67, moved from Idaho to Delaware to help care for her granddaughter. Galusha's decision comes as more families in the US are relying on grandparents for childcare. Grandparents provide childcare because of gaps in the childcare system, experts say.

Article Title: Kentucky man won $167.3 million Powerball jackpot in 2025; now arrested for fifth time after being found intoxicated in Walmart car park
Article Text:
Police found Kentucky Powerball winner asleep in a running Mustang

How James Farthing won Kentucky's record Powerball prize

Florida arrest came shortly after the jackpot win

February arrest involved an intimidation charge

Burglary and marijuana charges followed in March

July domestic violence case involved strangulation allegations

Fifth arrest adds to Farthing's legal cases

James Farthing, a Kentucky man who won a $167.3 million Powerball jackpot in April 2025, has been arrested for the fifth time since claiming the prize. The latest arrest took place on September 20, 2026, after deputies reportedly found him asleep inside a running Ford Mustang in a Walmart car park in Georgetown. Authorities charged him with being intoxicated in a public place following reports of alcohol-related impairment. The incident adds to a series of legal cases involving Farthing since his jackpot win. He had shared the historic prize with his mother, Linda Grizzle, after purchasing a $2 ticket from a Georgetown retailer.Earlier incidents included an April 2025 arrest in Florida, where Farthing was accused of kicking a sheriff’s deputy during an altercation. He later pleaded guilty to misdemeanor battery and obstruction or resisting arrest. In February 2026, he faced an intimidation charge, followed by burglary and marijuana-possession charges in March after being accused of entering a Lexington home and stealing $12,000. In July, he was arrested on domestic violence-related charges, including first-degree strangulation and fourth-degree assault. Farthing has pleaded not guilty to the domestic violence charges.The latest incident began shortly before 3 a.m. on Sunday, September 20, when a caller reported a white Ford Mustang stopped in the middle of an intersection in Georgetown, Kentucky. The vehicle later moved to a Walmart car park on Osborne Way, according to the arrest citation reported by WKYT.Deputies arrived and found the Mustang parked near an electric vehicle charging station with its engine running. Farthing was reportedly asleep in the passenger seat. Officers knocked on the window several times before he woke up.The arrest citation described several signs of impairment, including the smell of alcohol and marijuana, bloodshot and watery eyes, slurred speech and difficulty maintaining balance. Farthing was subsequently charged with being intoxicated in a public place and taken to the Scott County Detention Center.According to the arrest report, Farthing told deputies that a woman had driven him to the car park and left him there. Authorities reviewed surveillance footage, which reportedly showed no one exiting the Mustang after it entered the car park.Farthing purchased the winning Powerball ticket from Clark's Pump N Shop in Georgetown. The ticket matched the required numbers in the April 26, 2025 drawing, resulting in a $167.3 million jackpot.The Kentucky Lottery identified the prize as the largest Powerball jackpot ever won in the state. Farthing and his mother, Linda Grizzle, claimed the winnings together and announced that they would share the fortune.The win brought significant attention to the family, while Farthing later appeared in news reports concerning several encounters with law enforcement in Kentucky and Florida.Farthing's first reported arrest after winning the lottery took place in Florida in April 2025. Authorities accused him of battery involving a law enforcement officer and resisting arrest following an incident at a hotel.According to the Associated Press, officers said Farthing kicked a deputy in the face during an altercation and attempted to flee. He faced charges connected to the confrontation.The Independent later reported that Farthing pleaded guilty in the case and received a sentence of time served and $1,000 in fines.In February 2026, Farthing was arrested in Georgetown on a charge involving intimidation of a participant in a legal process. The case followed a report from a woman who contacted emergency services and said she feared for her safety.According to People, police investigated an incident at Farthing's home and reportedly found a woman hiding under a desk. Authorities also searched the property and allegedly discovered a handgun, ammunition, marijuana and drug paraphernalia.Farthing faced additional charges in March 2026 in connection with allegations of burglary and marijuana possession. Authorities accused him of entering a Lexington home and stealing approximately $12,000 in cash.The Guardian reported that investigators used security camera footage during the investigation. Farthing was later reportedly located at a casino.Local news reports said the burglary and marijuana charges were dismissed in May. The dismissal applied to those specific charges and did not resolve his other legal cases.In late July 2026, Farthing was charged with first-degree strangulation and fourth-degree assault following a reported domestic violence incident in Scott County.Police said a woman reported that a verbal argument became physical after a boating trip. According to the arrest report, she alleged that Farthing placed both hands around her neck and restricted her breathing. Authorities also reported visible marks on her neck.Farthing pleaded not guilty through his legal representative. A judge set his bond at $15,000 and ordered him to avoid contact with the alleged victim. He was also required to wear an electronic monitoring device with a notification feature.The September arrest is the fifth reported arrest involving Farthing since he won the Kentucky Powerball jackpot in 2025.The latest case concerns public intoxication in Scott County and follows the July domestic violence-related arrest. His legal proceedings remain separate from the lottery win, which he shared with his mother.As of September 23, 2026, the public intoxication case remained pending in Scott County District Court, with no confirmed outcome of the scheduled arraignment.The jackpot that promised a new beginning has instead been followed by a string of legal troubles. Fortune's wheel turns without warning, and wealth offers no guarantee of a steady life.
Article Summary: James Farthing won a $167.3 million Powerball jackpot in April 2025. He has been arrested for the fifth time since claiming the prize. The latest arrest took place on September 20, 2026, after deputies reportedly found him asleep inside a running Ford Mustang in a Walmart car park in Georgetown. Authorities charged him with being intoxicated in a public place following reports of alcohol- related impairment.

Article Title: In California, Fort Ord trained about 1.5 million soldiers; its former Army grounds now hold 86 miles of trails, wildflowers and mountain lions
Article Text:
Fort Ord National Monument view alongside wildflowers growing at Fort Ord. Credits - Wikipedia

Land formed by restricted access

A landscape for wildlife

Image of Old Coast Live Oak at Fort Ord. Credits - Wikipedia

An old battleground turned public sanctuary

Along California's Central Coast, large tracts of unspoiled coastal land are becoming less common as decades of urbanisation gradually fill in the open space between towns and highways. One noteworthy exception is located just outside of Monterey, where a former military facility that trained over a million soldiers has remained mostly intact due to decades of restricted military use that unintentionally preserved one of the last great wild landscapes in the area.Fort Ord was created by the US Army in 1917 as a field artillery training location along Monterey Bay and eventually became one of the largest Army installations on the West Coast. It served as an important staging area for forces headed to the Pacific during the next several decades, training soldiers prior to World War II, the Korean War and the Vietnam War. During its active years, Fort Ord was one of the largest training grounds in the country’s military history, with 1.5 million American troops passing through it, according to numbers supplied by the Bureau of Land Management. Ironically, the heavy military use protected most of the surrounding terrain from the kind of commercial growth that transformed other parts of the Monterey Peninsula. For much of a century the landscape remained closed to farming, housing and roadbuilding because huge portions of Fort Ord were live fire training zones and artillery ranges, allowing native grasslands, oak woods and marine chaparral to continue mostly undisturbed. When the facility finally shut down in 1994 under a government realignment scheme following the end of the Cold War, most of that area was left in a condition rarely seen elsewhere along the more populated California coast.Recognising the ecological and historic significance of what remained, President Barack Obama signed a proclamation in April 2012 designating about 14,651 acres of the former base as Fort Ord National Monument . The proclamation, signed under the authority of the Antiquities Act, permanently protected the property, citing both its unique ecological diversity and its significance to generations of American military service.Today the monument spans open meadows, dense stands of chaparral and oak woodland, connected by more than 86 miles of routes for walkers, bicyclists and equestrians. The terrain supports an extraordinary diversity of wildlife for a site so close to a major metropolitan area. Bobcats, coyotes, badgers, and mountain lions live in the area, along with rare and protected species such as the California tiger salamander and the Smith’s blue butterfly, one of the first insects in the country to be given a dedicated conservation reserve. Wildflowers dot the grasslands with the changing seasons, from the bright goldfields of spring to purple nightshade later in the year, attracting hikers and naturalists throughout the year.Managed by the Bureau of Land Management, the monument also has tangible vestiges of its military heritage, such as clearly designated and gated-off explosive ordnance areas, a relic of decades of service as an active training range. Visitors are requested to stay on authorised pathways to conserve vulnerable habitat and to avoid hazards still hidden in some portions of the landscape that have not yet been entirely removed.More than three decades after the last soldiers trained there, Fort Ord has become a silent counterpart to its own history, a site once marked by artillery fire and marching columns now defined by birdsong, wildflowers and the sounds of mountain bikes on packed dirt trails. The BLM is continuing to improve public access and trail infrastructure at the site, creating milestones that tie the monument’s military history to its present-day role as protected public property. The government said the site’s dual heritage will be part of a broader celebration of American service in 2026, when the very same ground on which soldiers prepared for war is now welcoming hikers, bikers and families experiencing one of California’s last vast expanses of open coastal wilderness.For a landscape that was closed to the public for much of the twentieth century, and shaped by the necessities of the military, the transformation of Fort Ord into a protected national monument is an unusual example of how sometimes it is not active conservation efforts that save a landscape, but the fact that it is inaccessible, allowing it to be saved long enough for permanent protection to catch up with it.

Article Title: In 2005, a California engineer used Google Earth to challenge a logging plan above Los Gatos Creek; community pressure later helped spare 1,000 acres of redwood watershed
Article Text:
Rebecca Moore used 3D satellite mapping to visualise a proposed logging area in the Los Gatos Creek watershed near Sierra Azul Open Space Preserve, helping local residents understand the scale and location of the project. Credits - Wikipedia, science.nasa.gov

Making sense of the map

The evidence offered

Rebecca Moore, Google Earth Outreach leader, speaks alongside Chief Almir of the Paiter-Surui people and members of the Surui community at a 2012 press conference in Rio de Janeiro, where Google launched the Surui Cultural Map. Credits - science.nasa.gov

A campaign that made a difference

Residents who oppose corporate development plans frequently find it difficult to understand complicated legal notifications and technical maps that unexpectedly arrive in the mail. When a group of landowners in the Santa Cruz Mountains of California got an official notification in 2005 detailing a proposal to chop a sizable area of forest above their homes, they found themselves in precisely that predicament. What transpired became one of the first instances of ordinary people using digital mapping technology to oppose a powerful organisation and alter the course of a local environmental battle.The warning was from the San Jose Water Company, a company that owns about 6,000 acres in the Los Gatos Creek watershed, a source of drinking water for more than 100,000 people in Silicon Valley. The company submitted a plan in August 2005 to cut about 1,000 acres of forest including coast redwoods and Douglas fir along a six-mile section of canyon, and copies of a black and white map explaining the plan were mailed to neighbouring people.For many, the document was almost impossible to comprehend as it gave little differentiation between roads, contour lines and the real borders of the proposed logging zone.One of the residents to get the warning was engineer Rebecca Moore, who was working on a mapping tool within Google that would become known as Google Earth Outreach . Instead of relying on the confused paper map, Moore set out to make her own map using satellite imagery and aerial pictures of the entire watershed. She helped create a neighbourhood group, Neighbours Against Irresponsible Logging, and utilised the new Google Earth software to map the proposed logging area much more accurately than the utility’s initial document had done.Moore’s computer map did more than map out boundaries. She layered in geo-located photographs of old-growth redwoods that stood in the way of the plan, added sightings of local wildlife such as ospreys and beavers, and imported data that showed that endangered red-legged frogs lived in the canyon, directly contradicting the company’s claim that no protected species were present. She also teamed with a colleague to build a three-dimensional flypast of a simulated helicopter carrying cut redwood trunks on a flight path over nearby schools and residences.Moore’s presentation of her flypast at the group’s inaugural community gathering had an instant impact. Residents who had failed to interpret a flat printed map could suddenly see, in three dimensions, how narrow mountain roads laced with more than 30 blind curves would convey a dozen 90,000-pound logging trucks each day past pathways frequented by children heading to school. The presentation gave the community a common and correct picture of exactly what the logging plan would do for their neighbourhood, which the initial notification had not provided.Separately, opponents of the plan objected to the size of the company’s assets. Residents said their own aerial surveys showed the company’s actual holdings exceeded a ceiling set by California law on the amount of commercially harvestable forest a single owner could hold and still qualify for the kind of open-ended logging permit the water company wanted. The issue was sent to California’s forestry regulator, which has standards for assessing proposals like these established by the CAL FIRE Board of Forestry and Fire Protection.Eventually community pressure and more regulatory issues pushed a turning point. By December 2007, almost two years after the original notice was mailed, the water company had withdrawn its logging proposal, and California’s forestry department had found the plan invalid under the laws that governed it. The result, for the redwood watershed above Los Gatos, was that some 1,000 acres of forest were saved from the large-scale cutting which the original plan had called for.The episode also had repercussions well beyond a small canyon in California. Moore’s success in using Google Earth to expose the difference between a company’s official map and the actual size of its plans became one of the origin stories for Google Earth Outreach, a programme designed specifically to help environmental and community groups use mapping technology in their own campaigns. Moore has said the fight above Los Gatos Creek influenced her later work creating tools to detect deforestation and environmental change across continents.Today, San Jose Water owns and manages thousands of acres in the same watershed and describes its approach to the property in terms of long-term stewardship rather than massive-scale timber harvesting. The 2005 controversy is one of the most startling early examples of how accessible digital mapping can shift the power from major institutions to locals, changing what may have been an intractable bureaucratic war into a contest that ordinary people could see clearly enough to win.
Article Summary: Rebecca Moore used 3D satellite mapping to visualise a proposed logging area in the Los Gatos Creek watershed near Sierra Azul Open Space Preserve. She helped create a neighbourhood group, Neighbours Against Irresponsible Logging, and utilised the new Google Earth software to map the proposed area.

Article Title: In 2025, a father and his 18-year-old son pushed a rowboat from San Francisco to Hawaii; nearly seven weeks and 2,400 miles later, they made history
Article Text:
Image of Tim Crockett and his son Harrison. Credits- Instagram/tamethekraken

A voyage beyond loss

Setting a record on arrival

Rainbow over the Pacific Ocean in Nuquí, Chocó, Colombia. Credits - Wikimedia Commons

Past the finish line

One of the most solitary sports in the world, ocean rowing requires participants to spend weeks by themselves on open water with nothing but oars and willpower. Few people ever do it, and even fewer decide to tell their family about the experience. An American father and his son completely altered the equation in the summer of 2025 when they set out from California to demonstrate that they could cross the Pacific Ocean together.The trip was launched by former member of Britain's Royal Marines Commandos and Special Boat Service, Tim Crockett, and his son Harrison, then 18. They set out from San Francisco Bay on 3 June 2025 in a 24-foot rowboat they christened The Kraken. Their destination was Hilo Bay on the Big Island of Hawaii, a crossing of almost 2,400 nautical miles of the Pacific, known by rowers as the Mid Pacific route. The campaign, called Tame the Kraken , had a purpose that went well beyond the physical challenge itself.Crockett’s link to ocean rowing was not sport, but sadness. Years before, a close buddy and fellow Special Forces man had taken his own life after dealing with the symptoms of post-traumatic stress. The death inspired Crockett to find a way to raise awareness for veterans’ mental health, and in 2018 he rowed solo across the Atlantic Ocean to achieve just that. The Pacific crossing with Harrison was meant to be a continuation of that effort, to promote a programme called Row to Recovery, which uses rowing as a kind of treatment for veterans suffering from impairments, PTSD and traumatic brain injuries.That aim affected how father and son undertook the voyage. They rowed in shifts, one always resting while the other pulled the oars. They faced weeks of relentless physical strain. They battled swells, exhaustion and rain that soaked their gear for days at a stretch. There were early moments when the enormity of the project nearly overwhelmed Harrison, he later said, remembering a moment when he just wanted to walk away. But their training and discipline through the expedition kept them going, oar stroke after oar stroke, over open ocean with no backup vessel behind.The physical demands were matched by extended spells of isolation, punctuated by occasional moments the duo would remember for the rest of their lives. One evening, as the sun was setting over the water, Harrison later recounted seeing a pod of dolphins swimming alongside the boat, calling it one of the most beautiful sensations of the voyage. There was a bit of a break from the monotony of rowing at least 12 hours a day in a boat that had no toilet and hardly enough room to sleep.Tim and Harrison Crockett rowed into Hilo Bay on July 20, 2025 after 47 days, 14 hours and 53 minutes at sea to become the first father and son pair to complete the Mid Pacific journey unaided. Crowds gathered at a hotel near the waterfront to welcome them, and the emotional reunion with Crockett's wife and daughter marked the end of a voyage that had pushed both men to their limits. Such ocean rowing records are recorded and certified by the Ocean Rowing Society International, the organisation that has been the official advisor on human-powered ocean crossings for many years, and the Crocketts have attempted to get their achievement recognised through that procedure.Their accomplishment also makes Harrison one of the youngest persons ever to finish a trans-Pacific row, a record that adds a new chapter to a sport better known for solitary veteran adventurers than for teenagers. For Tim, who had already demonstrated he could cross an ocean alone in 2018, rowing this trip with his kid brought an altogether new level of pressure, one based around safeguarding someone he loved rather than simply surviving hardship on his own.The end of the row was never the end of the narrative. The money donated during the voyage will assist in kickstarting Row to Recovery as a comprehensive recreational treatment programme centred in Atlanta, providing veterans with an organised outlet to use rowing as a physical activity and a contemplative focus. Tim Crockett said he thinks the repeated motion of rowing helps people stay completely present, which he says could help veterans manage the anxiety and hypervigilance that typically come with PTSD.Achievements of this scale are normally scrutinised by bodies like Guinness World Records, which works with ocean rowing authorities to validate new milestones after the paperwork and tracking information have been checked. That formal acknowledgement may or may not come. But the Crocketts have already done something unusual, turning a personal mission born of grief into a physical feat that took nearly seven weeks, thousands of miles and enormous trust between a father and his son to pull off.
Article Summary: Tim and Harrison Crockett rowed into Hilo Bay on July 20, 2025 after 47 days, 14 hours and 53 minutes at sea. They are the first father and son pair to complete the Mid Pacific journey unaided. Their accomplishment also makes Harrison one of the youngest persons ever to finish a trans-Pacific row.

Article Title: New Hampshire man returns a magazine 132 years late after library introduces fine freeze, avoiding a potential $12,055 fine
Article Text:
Image: Concord Public Library/ The Guardian

New Hampshire man discovers 1894 magazine in his home

Fine freeze encouraged overdue returns

The magazine dates back to September 1894

Library plans to preserve the historic return

An overdue library magazine has returned to its original home in New Hampshire after more than 132 years. John Hanson, an 84-year-old man from Barrington, recently brought a September 1894 issue of The Century Illustrated Monthly Magazine back to the Concord Public Library. The publication had remained in his home for decades, although he said he had no idea how it came into his possession. His decision to return it followed the library's introduction of a year-long fine freeze in September 2026. The initiative allowed him to avoid a potential $12,055 late fee, calculated from 48,220 overdue days. The unusual return surprised library staff and raised questions about the magazine's journey through more than a century of history.Hanson, a Concord native, had kept the magazine at home for decades. According to New Hampshire Public Radio, the item was initially in his Boscawen home before he moved to Barrington in 2010. He said he had no clear recollection of how it came into his possession. His father was born and raised in Concord but did not have a library card, leaving the original borrower's identity uncertain. Hanson speculated that he might have acquired it through a book pile or an advertisement sale.The Concord Public Library introduced a fine freeze on September 1, 2026, to encourage patrons to return overdue materials without accumulating additional penalties. The programme was announced as a year-long initiative to examine the effects of operating as a fine-free library. Hanson learned about the policy through a newspaper article and decided it was an appropriate time to return the magazine.The library said the magazine was 48,220 days overdue. At a theoretical rate of 25 cents per day, the resulting fine would have amounted to $12,055. However, Hanson did not have to pay the amount because of the fine freeze.The returned publication was an issue of The Century Illustrated Monthly Magazine, a periodical that combined literature, history and current affairs. The magazine included period advertisements and material reflecting social concerns of the late 19th century. The Guardian reported that the issue also contained writings associated with authors such as Mark Twain and Henry James.The magazine's original library markings included a bookplate and an instruction stating that it could be kept for one week. Its long absence has left library staff curious about the identity of the original borrower and the circumstances that led to its disappearance.The Concord Public Library does not plan to place the 1894 magazine back into regular circulation. Instead, staff said the issue could be preserved as part of the library’s historical collection or displayed in the Concord Room, where archival materials related to the city are kept. Its age, condition and connection to the library’s own history make it more than an ordinary overdue publication. After spending decades in private hands, the magazine could now serve as a physical record of the library’s past and of an era when such periodicals were routinely borrowed, read and returned. Its preservation would also allow future visitors to examine a publication that has survived for more than 130 years and has now returned to the institution that originally owned it.
Article Summary: John Hanson, 84, returned a September 1894 issue of The Century Illustrated Monthly Magazine to the Concord Public Library in New Hampshire. The magazine was 48,220 days overdue, which would have meant a fine of $12,055. The library introduced a fine freeze on September 1, 2026, to encourage patrons to return overdue materials.

Article Title: Pennsylvania's youth business fair grew from 60 booths in 2022 to 100 in 2026; kids ages 5 to 16 handled their own products, pricing and sales with no adults behind the tables
Article Text:
Representative image from Canva

A kitchen-table idea becomes a regional tradition

The rule that makes it real: no adults behind the table

How kids prepare their businesses

A marketplace of ideas and products

Judges, awards and encouragement

Part of a larger movement

Why this matters for families and schools

Poll Vote & Share your view What aspect of the Kidpreneurs Fair do you think benefits kids the most? Learning to manage money Gaining customer service skills Enhancing creativity 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Pennsylvania's youth business fair has grown from 60 booths in 2022 to 100 in 2026, turning a small community gathering into one of Central PA's most visible celebrations of kid-led enterprise. Children aged 5 to 16 run their own stalls, handling products, pricing, marketing and sales with no adults behind the tables, while parents and volunteers stay in the background as shoppers and supporters. The event, known as the Kidpreneurs Fair PA and hosted in Mechanicsburg, is part of the wider Acton Children's Business Fair network and is organised by local parents Ashruta Shettar and Pradeep Patil, who say the goal is to let kids learn entrepreneurship by doing rather than by watching, according to the fair's official site and the Children's Business Fair listing.The Kidpreneurs Fair PA began around a family kitchen table in 2022. Ashruta Shettar and Pradeep Patil, IT professionals and small-business owners, were watching their twin daughters dream up products and realised that their children would learn more by actually selling something than by talking about business in the abstract. They set up the first fair with 60 young entrepreneurs, offering each child a simple booth, a table and a chance to test their ideas with real customers.From that first event, the fair quickly became a local tradition. In 2024, participation grew to more than 85 kidpreneurs, with families turning out in large numbers to support everything from handmade crafts to original recipes. By 2025, nearly 160 children filled the marketplace, and some participants began converting their fair-day experiments into ongoing micro-businesses that operated beyond the single event. The 2026 edition capped booths at 100 and added a special touch, with personalised letters from the Governor of Pennsylvania for every participant, signalling how far the fair had come in just a few years.The most distinctive feature of the fair is its core rule. Parents may help with the application and with transport, but on fair day, children must run their own booths. They set up their displays, greet customers, explain their products, handle money and make change. Adults are welcome as shoppers and cheerleaders, but they are not allowed to sell or promote a child's product. If a parent is found doing so, the child's business can be disqualified from the competition.This rule is designed to give children an authentic experience of entrepreneurship. It means that a 6-year-old selling friendship bracelets must decide how much to charge, how to arrange the table and how to talk to strangers about their work. A 14-year-old offering custom keychains or baked goods must think about costs, profit margins and how to stand out in a busy marketplace. The fair becomes a safe space to make mistakes, learn from them and try again next year with a better plan.The application process itself is part of the learning. Children are asked to describe their product or service, set a price, estimate costs and explain how they will cover startup expenses. They must outline how they will advertise before the fair and how they will judge success at the end. Parents can assist with writing and calculations, but the expectation is that children do as much as possible on their own, appropriate to their age.Businesses are judged in six age categories, from 5 to 6 years old up to 15 to 16. Mixed-age groups are judged in the category of the oldest participant, and up to three children can share a single booth. The application fee is $35 per booth, fully refundable if the business is not accepted or if the family cancels at least a week before the event. Accepted applicants are notified on a rolling basis until the 100-booth cap is reached, creating a sense of urgency and planning for young founders.Walking through the fair feels like visiting a miniature version of a farmers market or craft fair, except every vendor is under 17. Booths feature handmade jewellery, slime and sensory toys, custom T-shirts, baked goods, art prints, pet treats, bath bombs and small services such as lawn care or tech help for neighbours. Some children build on hobbies, turning a love of drawing or baking into a branded product line. Others experiment with entirely new ideas, testing whether there is demand for a concept they have never tried before.Each business is given an 8-foot table, shared with one other vendor, under a tented outdoor setup at Messiah University's Eisenhower Campus Center in Mechanicsburg. Tablecloths are not provided, and electricity is not available, so children must design displays that work with simple materials. This constraint encourages creativity. A well-arranged table with clear pricing, attractive samples and a friendly pitch can make a big difference in how many customers stop and buy.A panel of local business leaders, educators and community figures serves as judges for the fair. Past and current judges have included school heads, CEOs of regional organisations, commissioners from state advisory bodies, owners of small businesses and representatives from major employers such as The Hershey Company and IKEA. They evaluate each business on creativity, presentation and entrepreneurial spirit, offering feedback that is meant to encourage young founders long after the fair ends.While prizes and recognition matter, the organisers stress that the real reward is the experience. Children leave with a clearer sense of what it takes to run a business, from costing and pricing to customer service and marketing. Some go on to expand their fair-day ventures into regular income streams, selling online or at local markets. Others simply gain confidence, realising that they can create something, put it in front of strangers and handle the entire transaction themselves.The Kidpreneurs Fair PA is part of the Acton Children's Business Fair network, which began in Austin, Texas, in 2007. That first event had just seven young entrepreneurs and about 25 attendees. Today, the Austin fair hosts more than 115 kidpreneurs and draws around 1,500 visitors, and similar fairs run in cities and towns across North America. The model is intentionally simple and replicable, relying on local hosts, volunteers and small sponsors to bring the experience to their own communities.In Pennsylvania, the fair is proudly sponsored by Sugaring NYC and supported by local donors and volunteers. The organisers say they believe principled entrepreneurs are heroes and role models for the next generation, whether they become famous business leaders or remain unsung owners of small neighbourhood enterprises. By giving children a structured, supportive environment to try entrepreneurship early, they hope to nurture a generation that sees business as a way to solve problems, serve others and build independence.For parents and educators, the fair offers a practical complement to classroom learning. Children apply maths when they calculate costs and profits, use language arts when they write product descriptions and signage, and practise social skills when they interact with customers. They also learn resilience. Not every product sells out, not every display attracts a crowd, and not every idea works the first time. Those lessons, experienced in a low-stakes setting, can shape how children approach challenges in school and later in work.As the Kidpreneurs Fair PA continues to grow, its organisers face choices about how big to go, how to maintain quality and how to keep the focus on learning rather than competition. For now, the trajectory from 60 booths in 2022 to 100 in 2026 suggests strong demand from families who want their children to have this kind of hands-on experience. In a region known for its small businesses and community spirit, the fair has become a place where the next generation can practise being founders, one table at a time.
Article Summary: Pennsylvania's youth business fair has grown from 60 booths in 2022 to 100 in 2026. Children aged 5 to 16 run their own stalls, handling products, pricing, marketing and sales with no adults behind the tables. Adults are welcome as shoppers and cheerleaders, but they are not allowed to sell or promote a child's product.

Article Title: 'White House access privilege, not right': DOJ cites national security behind Trump barring reporters
Article Text:
