File photo: An updated solidarity sign adding CNN, MSNOW and POLITICO hangs outside the Associated Press booth at the White House grounds after US President Donald Trump banned three major news outlets – CNN, MS

Also read:

What the DOJ is arguing

Also read:

Why did Trump revoke the hard passes?

Also read:

Press groups seek immediate restoration of access

The Trump administration has told a federal court that the president can restrict reporters’ access to the White House, including on the basis of their reporting, arguing that protecting national security gives him broad authority over who can enter the complex.In a court filing late Tuesday, the Justice Department argued that “access to the White House is a privilege, not a right” and said the administration could deny journalists access to restricted presidential areas even for “viewpoint-discriminatory reasons”.The filing came hours before an emergency hearing in Washington over the Trump administration’s decision to revoke the White House hard passes of CNN, MS NOW and Politico. The three news organisations are asking the court to restore their access.The administration has argued that the journalists’ reporting on sensitive and classified information has raised national security concerns.The Justice Department said the White House is a highly controlled government facility and argued that First Amendment protections do not give journalists an independent right to access it.Citing previous court rulings, the DOJ said the First Amendment does not create a right for journalists to enter the White House or obtain government information simply because they are members of the press.The filing also argued that the White House can impose standards on journalists receiving hard passes and that the president can determine whether reporters meet those standards.According to the filing, the administration considers the publication of classified or sensitive national security information a violation of the standards expected of journalists granted access to the White House.The DOJ said the government had two “compelling reasons” for restricting the journalists’ access: enforcing minimum standards of professionalism and protecting classified information.The administration also argued that the president has constitutional authority to protect information relating to national security. The filing cited a Supreme Court ruling recognising the president’s authority to classify and control access to national-security information.The DOJ further said the president had determined that reporting by the three organisations had threatened national security, including reports involving sensitive information about the White House complex.The White House press office said in letters to CNN, MS NOW and Politico that the president had decided to revoke their hard passes because they had allegedly violated standards of professionalism and decorum.The letters accused the organisations of publishing sensitive or classified information and, in some cases, spreading what the administration described as false information about national security.For CNN, the White House cited reports including a January story about construction details of a “top-secret” bunker beneath the White House east wing and an August report that US missile-defence interceptor stocks had been significantly depleted.The letter to Politico cited, among other reports, coverage of White House plans involving Secret Service security improvements and reports about US military weapons stocks.The MS NOW letter similarly cited reports involving alleged FBI leak investigations and US military munitions.The White House has given the three organisations until Friday to contest the decision and the factual basis cited in the letters.CNN, MS NOW and Politico have challenged the restrictions in federal court, arguing that the administration is retaliating against them because of their reporting.The dispute has already affected White House coverage, with major television networks, National Public Radio and White House photographers suspending or reducing live coverage in response to the restrictions, according to CNN.The federal court in Washington has previously intervened when administrations sought to restrict journalists’ White House access. The current case is therefore shaping up as a major test of how far presidential control over the White House extends when it comes into conflict with press freedom and due process protections.The emergency hearing before US district judge Timothy Kelly is expected to determine whether the three organisations will regain access while the broader legal fight continues.
Article Summary: Trump administration has told a federal court that the president can restrict reporters’ access to the White House, including on the basis of their reporting. The administration has argued that the journalists’ reporting on sensitive and classified information has raised national security concerns. CNN, MS NOW and Politico have challenged the restrictions in federal court.

Article Title: A 1954 Superman lunchbox sold for $31,980, beating its $20,000 high estimate at auction
Article Text:
PC: Morphy Auctions

The 1954 Superman lunchbox turned a school essential into comic-book merchandise

The Superman lunchbox stood out in a $1.8 million collectibles sale

PC: Morphy Auctions

Character lunchboxes from the 1950s and 1970s drew strong auction prices

Superman was only one of several major auction results

Marbles provided another unexpected high point

A metal lunchbox from the early years of Superman merchandise has become one of the notable vintage toy sales of 2026. The 1954 Superman lunchbox, complete with its matching Thermos and protective case, sold for $31,980 at Morphy Auctions’ Toys & General Collectables sale in June. The price was well above the auction house’s high estimate of $20,000, as per Morphy Auctions. Its value was tied to more than the Superman name. The lot brought together an early licensed lunchbox, original accessories and colourful period artwork, offering a surviving example of the kind of everyday object that carried comic-book characters into children’s lives during the 1950s.The lunchbox was manufactured by ADCO Liberty and released by Universal in 1954, when character-themed lunchboxes were beginning to establish themselves as a recognisable part of the children's market. Rather than being a plain container for a school meal, the metal box used lithographed artwork to turn the object itself into a piece of Superman merchandise.The auction lot included the Thermos as well as a protective case. That completeness helped distinguish it from a loose or incomplete example. The Superman graphics were also a major part of its visual identity, showing the Man of Steel in a confrontation with a giant gold robot against a city skyline.The Superman piece was one of 1,362 lots offered during Morphy’s Toys & General Collectibles auction, held on June 2 and 3, 2026. The wider sale generated more than $1.8 million, with vintage toys, sports memorabilia, marbles and other collectibles competing for attention.The Superman lunchbox was not the most expensive item in the auction, but its final price put it firmly among the sale’s notable results. It also formed part of a strong showing for the lunchbox category, which auctioneer Dan Morphy said had broken records alongside the soldier and marble categories.Morphy Auctions had placed a high estimate of $20,000 on the Superman lunchbox that ultimately sold for $31,980. It was not simply a high-priced vintage toy appearing in a major sale. The bidding pushed the final figure substantially beyond the upper end of the published estimate.The Superman result was part of a broader run of strong prices for vintage lunchboxes in the same auction. A mid-1950s Toppie the Elephant metal lithographed lunchbox sold for $16,605. It retained its matching Thermos, including the red cup lid, and came with two original Toppie companion books.A much later Underdog lunchbox, dating to around 1974, went further. The Leonard TTV metal example sold for $22,140 despite having some very mild surface scratches. Its condition was described as nearly mint overall, although the Thermos-Sew Thermos accompanying it was not original to the lunchbox.The Superman lot therefore sat in a wider group of character lunchboxes that attracted substantial prices. Its 1954 date, original Thermos and protective case gave it a different place within that group, while the artwork connected it directly with one of the best-known comic characters of the period.The June sale had plenty of competition outside the lunchbox category. A 1952 Topps Mickey Mantle rookie card sold for $51,660, matching the price achieved by a circa-1893 W Britains Germanic boxed set of royal fusiliers. The auction house described both as joint top lots.The W Britains set contained eight foot figures and a mounted officer and was housed in its original box. A first-version 275-piece W Britains Types of the British Army No. 131 set also performed strongly, selling for $41,820.The baseball material continued with a complete unopened 1972 Topps Series 3 wax box containing 24 factory-sealed packs, or 240 cards in total. That lot sold for $35,670, as reported.Marbles were another major part of the sale. A Christensen Agate No. 1 guinea box set containing 25 marbles sold for a record $49,200. The group included five blue-base guineas, seven amber guineas and 13 clear-base examples, nine of them cyclone guineas.Individual marbles also reached five-figure prices. A large green glass marble measuring 2-1/8 inches across sold for $29,520, while a sulphide marble featuring a painted rearing horse reached $27,060 against a high estimate of $6,000. A Joseph’s Coat clown marble brought $24,600.Against those results, the Superman lunchbox was part of a sale in which relatively ordinary-looking objects from earlier decades repeatedly became valuable because of their rarity, completeness and condition.
Article Summary: The 1954 Superman lunchbox sold for $31,980 at Morphy Auctions’ Toys & General Collectables sale in June. The price was well above the auction house’s high estimate of $20,000. The Superman result was part of a broader run of strong prices for vintage lunchboxes in the same auction.

Article Title: Super El Niño: California declares emergency as Hurricane Polo remains Category 5 off Mexico
Article Text:
A satellite image shows Hurricane Polo intensifying near the coast of southwestern Mexico. (Photo: CSU/CIRA & NOAA/Handout via REUTERS)

Polo remains Category 5 after winds peak at 285kmph

California, southwest Mexico face flood threat

US federal forecasts put the chance of a very strong El Niño above 90% this autumn and winter, with a 75% probability that the event could reach historic strength. California has declared a state of emergency ahead of the winter weather threat, while Hurricane Polo remains a Category 5 storm off Mexico.California Gov Gavin Newsom declared the emergency on Monday to mobilize resources before the El Niño peaks this winter. The order allows the state to position resources in advance and coordinate preparations for severe weather.California is likely to be among the US areas most exposed to the unusually strong climate cycle. Previous strong El Niño events have frequently brought damaging conditions to the state, while studies have associated them with above-normal precipitation, Cable News Network (CNN) reported.The effects are already being seen along the California coast, where El Niño has pushed sea levels higher. As the event reaches its expected winter peak, the state could face coastal flooding, heavy rainfall at lower elevations and mountain snow.Scientists regard widespread flooding along the coast as close to certain. El Niño can also add energy to waves generated by Pacific storms, increasing the risk of coastal erosion and closures on key transport links.Those coastal risks do not depend entirely on the path taken by major Pacific storms. El Niño itself raises coastal water levels, adding to sea-level rise already linked to climate change.The El Niño also coincides with the peak of an 18-year astronomical high-tide cycle. Patrick Barnard, research director at the Center for Coastal Climate Resilience at the University of California, Santa Cruz, said the cycle will push King Tides above their usual levels.Barnard said studies have found wave energy from Pacific storms to be about 30% higher during El Niño years. The increase reached as much as 50% during the 2015-16 event.He said a projected rise of about 15cm to 30cm in coastal water levels during the current El Niño could put another 170,000 people and $60 billion in property at risk compared with a non-super El Niño year.Off Mexico, Hurricane Polo remained at Category 5 strength on Tuesday after rapidly intensifying amid favourable atmospheric conditions and warmer water associated with the super El Niño.Polo's sustained winds peaked at about 285kmph at 3pm CST, when its minimum central pressure fell to 892mb, according to the National Hurricane Center. By 9pm, sustained winds had eased to about 270kmph and the hurricane was drifting northeast at about 2kmph. Its minimum central pressure had risen to 905mb, but it remained an “extremely dangerous” Category 5 storm.Between Monday and Tuesday morning, Polo's winds increased by about 175kmph, rising from around 80kmph as a tropical storm to about 260kmph at Category 5 strength.A storm meets the threshold for extreme rapid intensification when its wind speed rises by at least about 95kmph within 24 hours. The centre called Polo's rate of strengthening “truly remarkable” and said it was among the fastest recorded in the eastern Pacific.For comparison, Hurricane Patricia set the eastern Pacific 24-hour intensification record in 2015 with an increase of about 195kmph. In 2023, Hurricane Otis gained about 170kmph in 21 hours before hitting and devastating Acapulco.California could see flooding, mudslides and landslides as heavier precipitation combines with stronger storm waves.Newsom's emergency order directs agencies to prepare roads and other infrastructure, coordinate public-safety measures with local and tribal governments and pre-position equipment for flood response and snow removal. The California National Guard is also being readied for flood-response, search-and-rescue, engineering and logistics operations.A Tropical Storm Warning was in effect along Mexico's southwest coast from Tecpan de Galeana to Punta San Telmo. Polo's core was expected to remain offshore, but heavy rain posed a risk of life-threatening flooding and mudslides in Guerrero and Michoacán.Mexican authorities suspended classes in affected areas along the Pacific coast, the Associated Press reported.Reuters reported that authorities were monitoring the risk of rivers overflowing and had urged residents to stay away from flooded areas, secure loose outdoor items and plan routes to higher ground.Guerrero and Michoacán were forecast to receive about 8cm to 15cm of rain through Thursday, with isolated totals of up to 20cm. Coastal parts of Oaxaca, Colima and Jalisco could receive about 5cm to 10cm.
Article Summary: California, southwest Mexico face flood threat from El Niño. US federal forecasts put the chance of a very strong El Niño above 90% this autumn and winter. California has declared a state of emergency ahead of the winter weather threat. Hurricane Polo remains a Category 5 storm off Mexico.

Article Title: A volunteer sorting old Royal Navy papers found a rare 1776 US Declaration of Independence copy; it is one of 11 surviving Exeter printings and the only one outside the US
Article Text:
The copy of the 'Exeter Declaration' found at The National Archives.Photo credit: The National Archives

A chance find in a box of captains’ letters

The Exeter Declarations and why they are rare

How a Declaration ended up in British hands

Prize papers, procedure and a deliberate exception

The Dalton’s crew and their fate

Conservation and scientific examination

What the discovery means for historians

A new chapter in a 250-year story

A volunteer sorting old Royal Navy papers at The National Archives in London has uncovered a rare 1776 printing of the US Declaration of Independence, found among letters sent by a British captain after capturing an American privateer ship. The document is one of only 11 surviving copies printed in Exeter, New Hampshire, and is now the only known example outside the United States. Discovered in May 2026 by volunteer Michael Scurr while cataloguing Admiralty correspondence, the fragile broadside had travelled across the Atlantic as wartime evidence before resting quietly in a box of 18th-century naval letters for more than two centuries, according to The National Archives.The discovery came as part of the America 250 project, which is cataloguing Royal Navy admirals’ and captains’ letters from the American Revolutionary War to coincide with the 250th anniversary of US independence. Michael Scurr, a volunteer on the project, was working through a box of correspondence from Captain Thomas Fitzherbert of HMS Raisonable when he noticed a reference to documents seized from a captured American vessel.One item, described simply as “another paper,” turned out to be the Exeter printing of the Declaration.For Scurr, the moment was both thrilling and humbling. Handling a document that had helped announce the birth of a new nation, in the same year that the United States is marking its 250th anniversary, underlined how much history can still be hidden in plain sight within vast archival collections. His find shows how volunteers, working steadily through uncatalogued or under-examined records, can change what we know about major historical events.The Declaration of Independence was first adopted by the Continental Congress in Philadelphia on 4 July 1776. In the days that followed, printers across the Thirteen Colonies rushed to produce their own editions, spreading the news of independence as widely as possible. One of these printers was Robert Luist Fowle in Exeter, New Hampshire, who produced a small run of the text between 16 and 19 July 1776 for his newspaper, the New Hampshire Gazette or Exeter Morning Chronicle.These “Exeter Declarations” were printed quickly, on modest paper, for immediate distribution rather than long-term preservation. Over time, most copies were discarded, damaged or lost. Today, only 11 are known to survive, all held in US institutions until this discovery. The London copy is therefore unique not only for its rarity but for its location, offering a tangible link between the American Revolution and the British naval and governmental records that documented the conflict from the other side.The story of how this particular copy reached London begins with an American privateer named Dalton, a 20-gun brigantine commissioned by the Continental Congress to attack British shipping. In late 1776, the Dalton sailed from Newburyport, Massachusetts, with a mixed crew of about 120 men, including Americans, English, Irish, Scottish, French and Danish sailors, as well as at least one Black crew member, Daniel Cottle. During a stop on the Piscataqua River in New Hampshire, someone on board, most likely an officer, acquired a freshly printed Exeter Declaration.On Christmas Eve 1776, the Dalton was hunting for British prizes off the coast of Portugal when it encountered HMS Raisonable, a much larger 64-gun Royal Navy ship. After a seven-hour chase, the Dalton surrendered. Captain Fitzherbert recorded the capture in his log and took the American crew as prisoners. He then ordered one of his lieutenants to bring the Dalton, its senior officers and its papers into Plymouth for prize proceedings.Under British naval practice at the time, all papers found on a captured enemy ship had to be seized and presented to a prize court to determine whether the vessel and its cargo legally belonged to the enemy. The lieutenant acting as prize-captain swore that the only documents taken from the Dalton were its privateering commission and instructions from Congress. We now know that was not the full story.Captain Fitzherbert kept the Declaration for himself. He made copies of the Dalton’s commission and instructions and sent those to the Admiralty Secretary in Whitehall, along with a brief note mentioning signals and “another paper.” That “other paper” was the Exeter Declaration. By singling it out for immediate dispatch, Fitzherbert seems to have recognised its significance, even if Britain did not yet acknowledge the United States as a sovereign nation. From that point, the document remained within British government records, passing from the Admiralty to the Public Record Office and finally to The National Archives, where it lay unnoticed until 2026.The fate of the Dalton’s crew adds another layer to the story. After their capture, the sailors were imprisoned first on HMS Belleisle in Plymouth harbour and later at the Old Mill Prison, which by the end of 1779 held nearly 300 American prisoners. Among them was 19-year-old Charles Herbert of Newburyport, who kept a diary describing the harsh conditions and several escape attempts, including an elaborate tunnel dug beneath the prison.Herbert’s account reveals how the ideals of the Declaration played out in the lives of ordinary people. These men had volunteered to serve on a ship authorised by the Continental Congress, many of them attacking the shipping of their own nations of birth. Some were free Black sailors, others were immigrants or transient workers drawn into the conflict by opportunity, ideology or circumstance. Their experiences of capture, imprisonment and eventual release form a human counterpoint to the grand political claims of the document they carried.Once the Declaration was identified, collection care specialists at The National Archives undertook delicate conservation work. The document had been bound into a volume of Fitzherbert’s letters, attached with adhesive. Senior conservator Jillian Harrold used an ultrasonic humidifier to introduce moisture in a controlled way, softening the glue so the broadside could be gently separated with a spatula. A long tear across the middle was repaired using fine Japanese paper and wheat starch paste, stabilising the sheet for future handling and display.Heritage scientist Marc Vermeulen then examined the paper and printing. Raking light photography revealed the original fold lines, showing how the sheet had been handled and stored over time. Microscopic analysis detected blue fibres typical of rag paper made from recycled textiles, as well as yellowish plant fragments that may include hemp hurd. Transmitted light imaging showed the chain and laid lines characteristic of handmade paper, though no watermark was found. These features suggest a comparatively lower-quality paper, consistent with the urgent, economical printing conditions in wartime New England.For historians of the American Revolution, the Exeter Declaration in London is more than a rare printing. It is a physical trace of how the ideas of independence travelled across the Atlantic, carried on a privateer ship, captured by the Royal Navy and filed within British government records as evidence in a prize case. The document’s presence in Admiralty papers underscores how intertwined British and American histories were during the war, even as the two sides fought to define their future relationship.The find also highlights the continuing importance of archival cataloguing and volunteer-led projects. The America 250 initiative, building on earlier work to catalogue Royal Navy captains’ letters from the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars, created the conditions for this discovery. Without systematic attention to these boxes of correspondence, the Declaration might have remained hidden for decades more.The Exeter Declaration will feature in The National Archives’ exhibition Revolution 250: America’s Independence Story 1763–1783, which runs from June to November 2026. Alongside three Dunlap Broadsides, the first official prints of the Declaration held in the UK, the newly found copy offers visitors a chance to see different early printings and consider how the text circulated in its first weeks.For Michael Scurr and the team behind the America 250 project, the discovery is a reminder that major historical documents can still surface in unexpected places. A volunteer opening a box of 18th-century naval letters in London has added a new chapter to the story of the Declaration of Independence, linking a small New Hampshire print shop, an American privateer captured off Portugal and the British naval bureaucracy that preserved, perhaps unintentionally, a unique piece of transatlantic history.
Article Summary: The Declaration of Independence was first adopted by the Continental Congress in Philadelphia on 4 July 1776. printers across the Thirteen Colonies rushed to produce their own editions, spreading the news of independence as widely as possible. One of these printers was Robert Luist Fowle in Exeter, New Hampshire, who produced a small run of the text for his newspaper, the New Hampshire Gazette or Exeter Morning Chronicle. Over time, most copies were discarded, damaged or lost. Today, only 11 are known to survive, all held in US institutions.

Article Title: 'Almost all agents' data stolen? Hackers claim they breached FBI jobs site, stole 2TB of data
Article Text:
File photo: An FBI agent walks inside the front entrance of ex-Trump national security adviser John Bolton's Washington office (AP Photo)

What hackers claim they stole

Why did ShinyHunters target the FBI?

The FBI is investigating an apparent cyberattack on its job application website after the hacking group ShinyHunters claimed it stole more than 2 terabytes of data containing sensitive personal information about thousands of FBI employees and job applicants.The bureau confirmed that it was investigating unauthorised activity affecting FBIjobs.gov, while the website’s Special Agent applicant portal was unavailable on Tuesday.ShinyHunters claimed on its dark-web site that it had obtained “very sensitive data” on almost all FBI agents and people who had applied for jobs with the bureau. The group also claimed it had accessed the FBI’s criminal justice, human resources and other systems.However, Axios said it could not independently verify whether the stolen data was legitimate or current. Cybersecurity researchers told the publication that the attack itself appeared legitimate, while 404 Media obtained a sample of the alleged stolen data that appeared to contain information on about 5,000 people identified as FBI agents.According to Axios, ShinyHunters said the data included names, agent status, email addresses, phone numbers, home addresses and, in some cases, information about spouses, including Social Security numbers.The group also claimed it used a zero-day vulnerability in Oracle’s PeopleSoft platform to access and deface the FBI’s jobs website. The site remained offline on Tuesday afternoon.Cybersecurity experts told Axios that the potential exposure could pose a long-term risk to FBI employees and their families if the information is circulated among other criminal groups or sold on the dark web.Allan Liska, a threat intelligence analyst at Recorded Future, told Axios that the data was likely to be repeatedly downloaded and shared with other threat actors if it had been obtained as claimed.Andrew Brandt, principal threat intelligence incident commander at Huntress, said the biggest concern was whether ShinyHunters would sell the information to criminal or state-sponsored hackers.The group claimed the attack was not financially motivated. Instead, it demanded that the FBI retract or revise statements the bureau made about its activities.In a May advisory, the FBI warned that ShinyHunters commonly uses harassment tactics against victims and their families, including threatening calls and messages and, in some cases, swatting.ShinyHunters disputed the FBI’s description, telling Axios that other “low-skilled threat actors” had been carrying out attacks while using the group’s name.The FBI did not say whether it had confirmed the identity of the attackers or the extent of any data compromise.The incident comes as US law enforcement agencies face repeated cyberattacks. CNN reported that the FBI investigated a separate suspected breach in March involving a sensitive network used to manage wiretaps and intelligence surveillance warrants.Last month, hackers also leaked files they allegedly stole from the Justice Department’s Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives. CNN reported that the material appeared to contain sensitive information from past investigations.The FBI has also faced cyber incidents in the past, including a 2023 breach of a computer system used by its New York field office for child sexual exploitation investigations.
Article Summary: ShinyHunters claimed on its dark-web site that it had obtained ‘very sensitive data’ on almost all FBI agents and people who had applied for jobs with the bureau. The group also claimed it had accessed the FBI’s criminal justice, human resources and other systems.

Article Title: US-Iran talks: What was discussed in Trump's 'good meeting' on the sidelines of UNGA
Article Text:
US, Iran hold surprise talks through mediators as Tehran sets conditions to end war

What happened in the meeting

Trump warns Iran of 'annihilation'

War continues to pressure energy markets

US President Donald Trump said US and Iranian officials held an unexpected meeting on Tuesday, even as he warned in his address to the UN General Assembly that he could “annihilate” Iran if a deal is not reached soon to end the nearly seven-month war.Trump said his chief envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, held talks with Iranian officials for about three hours on the sidelines of the annual gathering of world leaders.Trump described the meeting as positive, saying, “It was a very good meeting.” He later added that the Iranian officials were “not the highest level, but it’s something.”US Middle East envoy Steve Witkoff said in a post on X that the talks were conducted through mediators who shuttled between the US and Iranian teams. He said he felt “very good” about the meeting and was hopeful the effort “will prove constructive and promising.”Iranian officials confirmed that foreign minister Abbas Araghchi took part in the talks, which were mediated by Qatari diplomats.Iran conveyed several conditions during the talks, including an end to the war on all fronts and a halt to what Tehran described as US “acts of aggression,” Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei told state news agency IRNA.Baghaei said Tehran also called for an end to the naval blockade and economic warfare, along with the release of Iranian assets, IRNA reported.A senior Iranian official separately said Tehran was prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within a week if Washington took reciprocal steps to ease military and economic pressure on Iran, as cited by the Guardian.The official said the position had been approved by Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei and the Supreme National Security Council.Earlier, the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) said there was no contradiction between pursuing negotiations and continuing the war. The position was also echoed by Iran’s chief negotiator Mohammad Ghalibaf in recent remarks to the Iranian parliament.The Iranian official said Tehran was looking for signs that Washington was prepared to resume negotiations, lift its military blockade of Iranian ports and halt operations linked to the Strait of Hormuz. If the US took those steps, Iran was prepared to reopen the strategic waterway within seven days and return to the negotiating table, the official said.However, some Iranian media outlets close to the IRGC denied that any new position had been adopted, highlighting differences within Tehran.In his address to the General Assembly, Trump defended his decision to launch the war with Iran, saying he had shown resolve while other leaders had hesitated.At the same time, he suggested the conflict could be approaching a turning point, calling on Iran to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz and return to negotiations to reach a settlement.“I have a big decision to make,” Trump said. “Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before, maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world. Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?”“The terrorist regime is behaving badly, not because they are strong and confident, but because they are weak and desperate," Trump added.Most members of Iran’s delegation walked out of the chamber as Trump criticised the Islamic Republic in his address.The conflict has grown more complicated despite US and Israeli strikes that have killed much of Iran’s top leadership and damaged its air force and navy, while a US blockade on Iranian oil has further strained Tehran’s economy.The war has also kept energy markets on edge, with oil prices remaining elevated. Earlier this month, Saudi Arabia shut a key pipeline that had served as an alternative route for oil stranded in the Gulf after it came under attack by Iran-backed militants in Iraq.Meanwhile, territorial advances by Yemen-based Houthi rebels, another Iran-backed group, near the Bab al-Mandab Strait have made the Red Sea shipping route increasingly hazardous for oil carriers.
Article Summary: Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi took part in the talks, which were mediated by Qatari diplomats. US Middle East envoy Steve Witkoff said he felt “very good” about the meeting and was hopeful the effort “will prove constructive and promising”

Article Title: Tennessee's Andrew Jackson estate spans 1,200 acres; its new plan puts much of a 70,000-square-foot visitor center underground so the building does not interrupt views across the historic landscape
Article Text:
Courtesy The Hermitage

Reimagining the historic landscape

Funding and public support

Expanding site interpretation and history

Plans for a $132 million redevelopment of The Hermitage, the 1,200 acre historic estate of former US President Andrew Jackson, will put much of a new 70,000 square foot visitor and education center underground to protect sightlines across the historic grounds. The Andrew Jackson Foundation announced the project, calling it a "generational transformation," to replace the current visitor facilities built in 1989. By placing large parts of the new complex underground, designers hope to keep views across the estate clear and help visitors feel like they've stepped back into the 19th century. Under the new site plan, called "Held by the Land," the redevelopment will change visitor paths, add a new tree-lined entrance, build an outdoor amphitheater, and restore historic spaces across the property, according to coverage by Nashville public radio station WPLN News.Located near Nashville, Tennessee, The Hermitage is a major presidential historic site holding roughly 800,000 artifacts and historic items. Project organizers said the current facilities no longer meet the needs of daily operations or storage for the collection. Leaders of the Andrew Jackson Foundation approved the full master plan to shift the estate's focus toward its natural surroundings. Putting the main education complex underground keeps modern buildings from towering over the fields and historic outbuildings nearby.Jason Zajac, president and chief executive officer of the Andrew Jackson Foundation, spoke about the responsibility of managing the site in an official statement released alongside the announcement. "The Hermitage is more than a presidential home. It is a place where some of the most consequential and complicated chapters of American history unfolded," Zajac said. "We have an immense responsibility to preserve this place while making sure the story we tell reflects the full history of the people who lived, worked and were enslaved here, as well as the nation shaped during Jackson's lifetime and presidency."The total cost of the project is estimated at $132 million, with most of the money expected to come from private donations. Public support has already started at the state level. Tennessee state lawmakers approved $6 million in funding to begin planning and early design work, as reported by WPLN News. Tennessee Governor Bill Lee spoke in support of the project in a statement about the historic property's educational value. "The Hermitage is an important part of Tennessee's history and helps tell the story of our state and our nation," Lee said.The physical redevelopment comes alongside ongoing efforts by the foundation to update how history is presented across the 1,200 acres. In recent months, site historians have been updating guided tours, including the "In Their Footsteps" program, which focuses on the lives of people enslaved on the plantation. As noted in earlier reporting by WPLN News, these updates aim to give a fuller picture of the enslaved men, women, and children who lived and worked at The Hermitage. The new visitor and education facility will include larger gallery spaces and research areas to better display artifacts and share these connected histories with the public. A timeline for building and finishing the new underground complex will be set as design work moves forward.
Article Summary: A $132 million redevelopment of The Hermitage will put much of a new visitor and education center underground. The Andrew Jackson Foundation announced the project, calling it a "generational transformation" The redevelopment will change visitor paths, add a new tree-lined entrance, build an outdoor amphitheater.

Article Title: Gunmen kill 2 cops during polio vaccination drive in Pakistan's Balochistan
Article Text:
(Representative image): The officers had been deployed to protect the vaccination team, which was carrying out the weeklong immunisation campaign launched by the government on Monday.

Police officers killed during vaccination drive

Pakistan remains polio hotspot

Gunmen shot dead two police officers protecting polio vaccination workers in Pakistan's southwestern Balochistan province on Tuesday. The officials said that the attack took place as health teams carried out a door-to-door campaign targeting more than 31 million children.The gunmen opened fire when Nushki district, polio workers were administering oral vaccine drops to children inside a home. The health workers escaped unharmed, local police official Munawar Zaman said.No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack.The officers had been deployed to protect the vaccination team, which was carrying out the weeklong immunisation campaign launched by the government on Monday.The latest campaign aims to vaccinate more than 31 million children across Pakistan against polio.Balochistan has faced repeated attacks by militant groups, including separatist militants. The Pakistani Taliban has also previously targeted security forces and civilians in Balochistan and other parts of the country.Pakistan's interior minister Mohsin Naqvi condemned the attack in a statement.Pakistan and neighbouring Afghanistan are the only countries where transmission of wild poliovirus has not been interrupted, according to the World Health Organisation.Security concerns have repeatedly complicated vaccination efforts in Pakistan, with polio workers and the police personnel assigned to protect them facing attacks during previous campaigns.
Article Summary: Gunmen shot dead two police officers protecting polio vaccination workers in Pakistan's southwestern Balochistan province. The officers had been deployed to protect the vaccination team, which was carrying out the weeklong immunisation campaign launched by the government on Monday. No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack.

Article Title: 'Mass casualty' alert? Pakistan hospitals clear beds ahead of PTI protest
Article Text:
Protests in Pakistan (Representative image)

Imran Khan's family detained

Hospitals in Islamabad have allegedly been ordered to prepare for a possible “humanitarian crisis” and “mass casualty incident” ahead of a planned September 27 protest by jailed former Pakistan prime minister Imran Khan’s party, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI).The instructions to Islamabad hospitals called for all scheduled elective surgeries to be postponed indefinitely and surgical departments to be prepared for a possible surge in patients, according to documents reviewed by Drop Site.Medical and support staff were ordered to remain available, with all forms of leave suspended. Hospitals were also told to recall employees who were already on leave.The measures were issued ahead of PTI’s planned September 27 march, which the party says is intended to demand Khan’s release.The preparations have already affected patients. People familiar with the situation told Drop Site that patients scheduled for surgery on Monday were informed that their procedures would be postponed.The government has not publicly said that the hospital preparations are specifically linked to a crackdown on PTI protesters. The documents, however, explicitly refer to preparations for a potential “humanitarian crisis” and “mass casualty incident”.The hospital preparations also came as authorities detained Khan’s three sisters – Aleema Khan, Noreen Niazi and Dr Uzma Khan – along with other members of his family, while several PTI leaders and workers were also arrested ahead of the planned march on Islamabad.Eight members of Khan’s family were reportedly detained within 24 hours. The children were later released after several hours, according to Aleema Khan’s son Shershah Khan, while Khan’s sisters remained in custody.Aleema Khan was detained under Section 3 of Pakistan’s Maintenance of Public Order law, with a formal order issued by Lahore’s deputy commissioner authorising her detention for 30 days, according to documents obtained by Drop Site.Similar detention orders circulated for Noreen Niazi and Uzma Khan.The arrests came after authorities stepped up action against PTI members ahead of the September 27 mobilisation. PTI has alleged that party offices were raided and elected representatives and workers were detained across the country.The arrests have come amid continuing concerns from Khan’s family and supporters over his health and prison conditions.Khan’s primary healthcare provider, Dr Faisal Sultan, has reportedly not been allowed to visit him for several weeks. Khan has been imprisoned since August 2023 after his government was removed from office following a no-confidence vote. PTI has continued to demand his release.
Article Summary: Imran Khan's party, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI), plans to march on Islamabad on September 27. Hospitals in Islamabad have been ordered to prepare for a possible ‘humanitarian crisis’ and ‘mass casualty incident’ All scheduled elective surgeries have been postponed indefinitely.

Article Title: Pakistan in crisis: PTI to hold Sept 27 stir 'at all costs'; Imran Khan's sisters challenge detention orders
Article Text:
Pakistan: Imran Khan's sisters challenge detention orders in court, demand immediate release

PTI says September 27 protest will go ahead

Family condemns detentions

Pakistan's opposition Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) will proceed with its planned September 27 protest demanding the release of jailed former prime minister Imran Khan, even as legal challenges have been filed against the preventive detention of his three sisters.A petition was filed in the Lahore High Court on Monday challenging the 30-day detention orders issued against Aleema Khan, Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi, according to a report by Pakistan-based daily The Express Tribune, as cited by news agency ANI.The petition, filed by Shahraiz Khan, son of Aleema Khan, seeks to have the detention orders declared invalid and the immediate release of the three women.The detention orders were issued by the Lahore deputy commissioner on September 20 under Section 3 of the Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance, ahead of PTI's planned September 27 demonstrations.Aleema Khan was detained earlier, while Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi were detained on Monday.The petition alleged that Aleema Khan was intercepted while travelling for personal errands and that there was no public gathering or situation at the time that could pose a threat to public order. It also stated that Aleema Khan and her driver, Muhammad Ameer, were being held at Lahore Central Jail.The petitioner described Aleema Khan as a law-abiding individual and alleged that the detention order did not contain specific allegations justifying preventive detention.The respondents named in the petition include the home department secretary, Lahore deputy commissioner, capital city police officer and Lahore Central Jail superintendent, according to The Express Tribune.Khyber Pakhtunkhwa chief minister Sohail Afridi said on Monday that PTI would go ahead with its September 27 protest “at all costs”. He said the party would announce its detailed protest plan on September 25 and mobilise workers across Pakistan.Afridi said arrests of PTI provincial ministers and lawmakers had begun ahead of the protest, prompting an emergency meeting of the party's parliamentary group.He said the party had pursued “all constitutional and democratic avenues” but was being prevented from meeting Imran Khan despite court orders.Afridi said PTI had no intention of confrontation and would pursue its demands through peaceful and democratic means. He also said party workers would not carry weapons during the protest.PTI chairman Barrister Gohar said the party was not planning to “storm” Islamabad and would not take the law and order situation into its own hands. He said the authorities were provoking the party but PTI would not come to Islamabad “like terrorists”.Interior minister Mohsin Naqvi, meanwhile, said the government would not allow the September 27 protest to disrupt Islamabad. Speaking to reporters in Lahore on Monday, he said preparations were under way for an “assault” and that the government would not allow the capital to be shut down.Imran Khan's son, Kasim Khan, also condemned the detention of his relatives and appealed for international intervention.In a post on X, he said, “This is a disgrace. Now my Aunts Dr Uzma and Noreen, along with my cousins Shershah and Shahrez, have now been abducted as well. They have broken into my aunties' and cousins' houses and forced them into vehicles with no explanation. No reasons for arrest have been stated.”He added, “No news has been released as to where they have been taken. This is criminal behaviour. Inexcusable. The Pakistani people are petrified of their own leaders. No upstanding nation should tolerate this criminal establishment. Intervention is now imperative. The world MUST take action.”The arrests come as PTI prepares for the September 27 protest seeking the release of Imran Khan, who has been in jail since 2023 and is currently held at Adiala Jail in Rawalpindi.
Article Summary: A petition was filed in the Lahore High Court on Monday challenging the 30-day detention orders issued against Aleema Khan, Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi. The petition, filed by Shahraiz Khan, seeks to have the detention orders declared invalid and the immediate release of the three women. Imran Khan's son Kasim Khan also condemned the detention of his relatives and appealed for international intervention.

Article Title: 'PTI's drama will never achieve anything': Pak minister Naqvi warns Imran Khan's party ahead of Islamabad march
Article Text:
Mohsin Naqvi warns Imran Khan's PTI

Also Read:

(With agency inputs)

Pakistan interior minister Mohsin Naqvi on Monday warned jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) ahead of the party’s planned protest in Islamabad, saying it “can never achieve anything through such drama. "The PTI plans to march towards the capital on September 27 to demand the release of its founder Imran Khan, who has been in jail since 2023 after being arrested following his conviction in a corruption case. Currently, the cricketer-turned-politician is lodged at the high-security Adiala Jail in Rawalpindi.“We will not allow PTI to enter Islamabad and shut down the city for several days. We have clearly told them that they can never achieve anything through such drama, and I will say again that there is still time; they should not go into this situation,” Naqvi told reporters.He also referred to an Islamabad high court order directing the federal government to ensure peace in the capital and claimed that a majority of PTI leaders did not support the planned protest.“Do not harm yourself and your workers,” he told the PTI leadership, urging it to adopt a “different approach”.Asked about measures to find a long-term solution to the PTI’s repeated protests, Naqvi replied, “This time we will find a permanent solution; we will not leave it halfway.We can't afford this every time.”On reports of a possible ban on the party, he said the government would seek a “once-and-for-all solution.”Meanwhile, the federal government was stepping up security measures ahead of the protest, including placing shipping containers along roads and bringing in police personnel from other provinces.More than 22,000 security personnel, led by eight senior police officers, were to be deployed in Islamabad, while more than 30,000 were to be stationed in Attock district, which connects Khyber Pakhtunkhwa with Punjab.Police in Rawalpindi, Islamabad’s twin city, have separately sought 9,000 additional personnel to assist the local administration.The PTI is not the only group planning protests in Islamabad. Right-wing Jamaat-e-Islami launched a demonstration against rising petroleum prices on Sunday and was heading towards the capital from Karachi.The Kissan Ittehad farmers’ group has also announced a sit-in in the city this week, seeking relief for farmers.
Article Summary: Mohsin Naqvi warns Imran Khan's PTI ahead of planned protest in Islamabad. Interior minister says party "can never achieve anything through such drama" Federal government stepping up security measures ahead of the protest. More than 22,000 security personnel, led by eight senior police officers, to be deployed.

Article Title: 'Broke into house, forced them into vehicles': Imran Khan’s son alleges aunts, cousins 'abducted' in Pakistan
Article Text:
Pakistani Police has already arrested ex-PM Imran Khan's sister in Lahore ahead of party's planned march. (Reuters photo)

More relatives allegedly detained

Aleema's detention ahead of PTI march

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you believe that the recent detentions of PTI members are politically motivated? Yes, definitely No, they're justified 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Days before Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf's planned September 27 protest march, former prime minister Imran Khan 's son Kasim Khan has alleged that several members of his extended family have been detained and that their whereabouts have not been disclosed.In a series of posts on X, Kasim alleged that his aunts Dr Uzma and Noreen, along with cousins Shershah and Shahrez, were taken from their homes after authorities allegedly entered the properties and forced them into vehicles. The claims could not be independently verified.“This is a disgrace. Now my Aunts Dr. Uzma and Noureen, along with my cousins Shershah and Shahrez have now been abducted as well,” Kasim said.“They have broken into my aunties and cousins houses and forced them into vehicles with no explanation. No reasons for arrest have been stated. No news has been released as to where they have been taken,” he alleged.Kasim described the alleged detentions as “criminal behaviour” and called for international attention to the matter.Kasim later said the two children of Shahrez, aged four and six, had initially been missing. He subsequently said the children were safe but alleged that two more cousins, Azeem and Sakeenah, had also been taken into custody.“Hearing news that my cousin’s children are now safe. Meanwhile, two more of my cousins have been arrested. Azeem and Sakeenah. No reasons given. No location given,” he said.The allegations follow the detention of Imran Khan's sister Aleema Khan in Lahore on Sunday. She was ordered to be held for 30 days under the Punjab Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance, with the authorities citing public safety and order concerns. She was later taken to Kot Lakhpat jail, according to police and Pakistani media reports.Lahore deputy commissioner Muhammad Ali Ijaz issued the detention order under the MPO law. The order cited allegations involving protests, roadblocks and the mobilisation of PTI workers.PTI chairman barrister Gohar Ali Khan condemned Aleema's detention and demanded her release, arguing that it could further increase tensions ahead of the September 27 demonstration.Aleema's son Shahrez had earlier alleged that his mother was “abducted” after leaving her home and said the family had no information about where she had been taken.The PTI march is being organised to demand the release of Imran Khan, who remains in jail and is facing multiple legal cases. Pakistani authorities have stepped up measures against PTI supporters ahead of the planned protest.Meanwhile, Pakistani media have reported that Imran Khan underwent a medical check-up in jail amid continuing concerns raised by his family over his health.The government has cited public-order concerns in relation to Aleema Khan's detention, while PTI and members of Imran Khan's family have disputed the action and demanded information about those taken into custody.
Article Summary: Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf's planned September 27 protest march. Imran Khan's son Kasim Khan has alleged that several members of his extended family have been detained and that their whereabouts have not been disclosed. The allegations follow the detention of Imran Khan's sister Aleema Khan on Sunday.

Article Title: Pakistan airstrikes on Afghanistan: 3 killed, several injured as conflict fears grow
Article Text:
Relations between Kabul and Islamabad have remained strained over militant activity along border. (AP photo/ File)

Taliban warns of 'crushing response'

Kabul denies sheltering TTP

Afghanistan keeps door open for talks

Poll Vote & Share your view What should be the main focus for Pakistan and Afghanistan in resolving their issues? Diplomatic negotiations Border security Intelligence sharing Ceasing cross-border operations 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

At least three people were killed and several others injured in a Pakistani airstrike targeting Afghanistan's northeastern Kunar province, Tolo News reported on Monday, citing a provincial official.The military strike is supposedly in retaliation for suicide bombing at a police station compound in northwestern Pakistan, raising fears that tensions between the neighbouring nations could once again turn into open fighting.Pakistan and Afghanistan were involved in their most serious military confrontation in years in February. The latest escalation comes days after the Taliban warned that it would defend Afghan territory against any Pakistani military action.Taliban spokesperson Zabihullah Mujahid, ahead of the imminent Pakistani strikes, had warned Islamabad against carrying out strikes inside Afghanistan, saying Kabul would respond militarily if its territory is attacked.In an interview with Al Arabiya English, Mujahid rejected Pakistan's allegations that militant groups based in Afghanistan recruit, train and launch attacks against Pakistan.“If Pakistan invokes Article 51 to violate the sanctity of Afghan territory, Afghanistan has the right to defend its country, and we will do so,” Mujahid said.He said any Pakistani military operation inside Afghanistan would amount to a violation of Afghan sovereignty and could trigger a strong response from Kabul.Mujahid was responding to comments by a Pakistani military spokesperson, who had told Al Arabiya English that militant groups were using Afghan territory to recruit, train and arm fighters before sending them into Pakistan.Mujahid rejected those allegations and said the Taliban administration does not allow the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan , or TTP, to operate from Afghan soil.He also denied that the Taliban government supports armed groups carrying out attacks against other countries. Instead, Mujahid said Pakistan should examine its own internal security problems, arguing that violence involving the TTP and Baloch armed groups existed before the Taliban returned to power in 2021.Pakistan has repeatedly accused militant groups of operating from Afghanistan and has pressed Kabul to take action against them. The Taliban has consistently denied allowing Afghan territory to be used for attacks against Pakistan.Despite his warning of military retaliation, Mujahid said Kabul was still willing to engage with Islamabad through dialogue.He called for stronger intelligence-sharing arrangements and greater bilateral cooperation to address security concerns along the two countries' border.Mujahid also backed a possible mediation role for Saudi Arabia, saying Riyadh has good relations with both Afghanistan and Pakistan and could help the two sides resolve their differences.Relations between Kabul and Islamabad have remained strained over militant activity along their shared border. The latest airstrike, coming amid fresh security concerns, risks further worsening those ties and could lead to another confrontation between the neighbours.
Article Summary: Pakistan and Afghanistan were involved in their most serious military confrontation in years in February. The latest escalation comes days after the Taliban warned that it would defend Afghan territory against any Pakistani military action. Relations between Kabul and Islamabad have remained strained over militant activity along their shared border.

Article Title: Pakistan braces for protests as govt warns of $400 million daily loss
Article Text:
Protests in Pakistan (Representative image)

Government warns of economic fallout

Islamabad steps up security

Pakistan’s government has put heavy restrictions on protestors warning them that those seeking to march towards Islamabad with the government warning that disruptions could cost the economy around $400 million a day as separate marches by Jamaat-i-Islami (JI) and Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) put pressure on the capital.Pakistan’s information minister Attaullah Tarar said on Sunday that the administration, police and interior ministry were clear that groups intending to cause disruption would not be allowed to reach the capital. He cited a recent Islamabad high court ruling that bars political parties from obstructing public roads and the movement of citizens.The warning comes ahead of a PTI nationwide protest and march towards Islamabad on September 27 seeking the release of party founder Imran Khan, who is incarcerated. JI, meanwhile, has launched a protest campaign against the petroleum levy and has begun a march towards the federal capital.Pakistan’s finance minister Muhammad Aurangzeb separately warned that strikes, sit-ins, long marches and road closures could cause an estimated PKR 120 billion (over $400 million) loss to Pakistan’s economy every day.According to estimates prepared by the planning commission and finance ministry, the services sector, including financial services, communication, retail, transport, wholesale and hospitality, could account for about PKR 86 billion of the daily loss.Industry could lose PKR 25 billion and agriculture PKR 9 billion, while the government could face an additional revenue loss of around PKR 17 billion.Aurangzeb said the disruption would come at a time when businesses were already dealing with higher freight and insurance costs and supply-chain problems linked to tensions in the Middle East, including disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab.He also warned about the impact on IT exports. Pakistan recorded $811 million in IT exports during July and August, he said, adding that previous internet disruptions during episodes of civil disobedience had affected IT exports by as much as 80%.Authorities have begun preparing for the potential marches, with hundreds of containers placed at entry points to Islamabad. Police officials have also reviewed security arrangements at major entry and exit points and other sensitive locations.The Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences and Federal Government Polyclinic Hospital have been placed on high alert, with emergency, trauma, ICU, operating theatre, blood bank and ambulance services instructed to remain fully operational. Pims said the arrangements would remain in place until September 30.The government has also cited concerns over statements by PTI leaders about the planned march. Pakistan’s parliamentary affairs minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry said a reported remark by a senior PTI leader about turning Islamabad into “Somnath” had raised concerns about possible violence. He said the government had a responsibility to maintain law and order in the capital.The government has said it remains in contact with JI leadership and hopes to resolve the dispute through dialogue. JI has been protesting since August 16 against the petroleum levy and says it wants the government to withdraw the levy.
Article Summary: Jamaat-i-Islami (JI) and Imran Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek- i-Insaf (PTI) put pressure on the capital. JI has launched a protest campaign against the petroleum levy and has begun a march towards the federal capital. Government warns that strikes, sit-ins, long marches and road closures could cause an estimated PKR 120 billion (over $400 million) loss to Pakistan's economy every day.

Article Title: Jailed former Pak PM Imran Khan undergoes medical check-up amid concerns over health
Article Text:
Imran Khan

Geo News

Jailed former Pakistan prime minister Imran Khan underwent a medical check-up at Adiala Jail amid concerns over his health, according to a media report on Sunday.Khan, 73, has been in jail since 2023 following his conviction in a corruption case and is currently lodged at the high-security Adiala Jail in Rawalpindi.According to, a specialist team from the state-run Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) examined Khan at the jail. The check-up included assessments of his blood pressure, cholesterol levels and eyesight.The medical team was led by a PIMS doctor, with medical staff from the Adiala Jail hospital assisting during the examination, the report said.Khan has previously complained of an eye condition and has been taken to PIMS several times for treatment. His supporters have alleged that his health has deteriorated due to inadequate medical care, a claim that prison authorities have repeatedly rejected.The Supreme Court had ordered on August 18 that Khan be shifted to a private medical facility for treatment. However, he was taken to PIMS, where he underwent medical tests before being returned to jail, news agency ANI cited.His Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party has sought his transfer to Islamabad's Shifa International Hospital for a detailed medical examination and treatment, while raising concerns over his health.The party has also announced a September 27 demonstration seeking Khan's release.Khan has faced multiple legal cases since his removal as prime minister through a no-confidence vote in April 2022, with his health and conditions of detention remaining a recurring issue in Pakistan's political discourse.
Article Summary: Imran Khan, 73, has been in jail since 2023 following his conviction in a corruption case. Khan has previously complained of an eye condition and has been taken to PIMS several times for treatment. His supporters have alleged that his health has deteriorated due to inadequate medical care.

Article Title: Ex-Pakistan PM Imran Khan's sister Aleema arrested in Lahore ahead of Sept 27 PTI march
Article Text:
Aleema Khan arrested ahead of planned Imran Khan-founded PTI march

Long-imprisoned former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan 's sister, Aleema Khan, was arrested from her home in Lahore on Sunday ahead of a planned march on September 27.Police arrested Aleema as she was planning a protest march organised by Imran Khan-founded Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI). A PTI spokesperson confirmed her arrest to Reuters.A notification issued by Lahore's district administration said Aleema Khan had been arrested and sent to jail for 30 days, citing concerns over public safety.“According to intelligence reports, her presence at any public place will pose a grave threat to public safety,” the notification said.Imran Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) has planned a march to Islamabad next week, demanding the former prime minister's release.Pakistan interior minister Mohsin Naqvi said on Saturday that the government would take all possible measures to prevent the protest march.Zulfi Bukhari, a close aide to Imran Khan, condemned Aleema's arrest as “absolutely despicable”.“The fear of the 27th protest is clearly taking its toll,” Bukhari said.The World Cup-winning cricket captain and former prime minister Imran Khan has been imprisoned for more than three years.Khan's family, including his two sons, have repeatedly expressed concern over his health and alleged a conspiracy involving Pakistan's de facto leader and military chief Asim Munir.
Article Summary: Aleema Khan arrested ahead of planned Imran Khan-founded PTI march. Imran Khan's sister sent to jail for 30 days, citing concerns over public safety. Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) has planned a march to Islamabad next week.

Article Title: Pakistan foreign minister dials Iranian counterpart, urges uninterrupted energy supplies and safe passage of ships
Article Text:
Abbas Araghchi and Ishaq Dar (File photo)

(With PTI inputs)

Pakistan’s foreign minister Ishaq Dar on Saturday urged his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, that Tehran must ensure “uninterrupted energy supplies” and the “safe and expeditious passage of ships”, amid concerns over disruptions to crucial waterways in the Middle East.Dar, who also serves as Pakistan’s deputy prime minister, held a telephonic conversation with Araghchi to discuss the latest regional developments, according to a statement from Pakistan’s Foreign Office (FO) on X.During the call, Dar “stressed the importance of uninterrupted energy supplies and the safe and expeditious passage of ships, particularly given their implications for developing countries and global supply chains”.He also underscored that “dialogue and diplomacy remain the only viable means to ensure peace and stability in the region”, the FO noted.The two ministers agreed to maintain close cooperation and meet in New York City next week on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, the foreign office added.The conversation came amid growing concerns over the safety of oil supply routes as tensions escalate around the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb, as well as uncertainty surrounding the United States-Iran war, which began on February 28.The Strait of Hormuz links the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman, while Bab al-Mandeb connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden.The Strait of Hormuz has been under a virtual Iranian blockade since March, with Tehran effectively restricting passage through the critical maritime corridor in retaliation for US-Israeli attacks on Iran that triggered the conflict.Meanwhile, Yemen’s Houthi forces, aligned with Tehran, have imposed a de facto blockade on the Bab al-Mandeb Strait since July, seizing key shoreline territory and Mayun Island while specifically targeting Saudi-linked shipping and energy infrastructure.
Article Summary: Pakistan’s foreign minister Ishaq Dar urged his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, that Tehran must ensure ‘uninterrupted energy supplies’ Dar also underscored that “dialogue and diplomacy remain the only viable means to ensure peace and stability in the region’

Article Title: 'We want to go home': Hindu minor sisters abducted, converted, married in Pakistan's Sindh
Article Text:
Pakistan: Two minor Hindu sisters allegedly abducted, converted and forced into marriage

Sindh at centre of concern over minority girls

The alleged abduction and forced conversion of two minor Hindu sisters in Pakistan's Sindh province has triggered fresh concern among minority rights group, with one organisation calling for an independent probe and safeguards for the girls.According to Voice of Pakistan Minority, Roopi, 13 and Seeta, 14, were allegedly taken from Ibrahim Colony in Tando Allahyar district and later converted to Islam and married to two Muslim men, Amjad Solangi and Mansood Solangi.The sisters were subsequently brought before a court in Tando Allahyar in an abduction case. Instead of sending them back to their family, the court placed them in a safe house, VOPM said.The rights group said the girls appeared distressed outside the court and were heard pleading to be taken home. A video circulating online also purportedly showed the sisters saying, “Let us go to our parents” and “We want to go home.”VOPM said the circumstances surrounding the case made it important that the sisters be heard independently, without anyone who could influence or intimidate them.“The state must interview Roopi and Seeta in a child-sensitive environment, away from alleged husbands, religious figures, intermediaries or anyone who could pressure them.Officials must allow the girls to speak freely and must provide them independent legal support and protection,” VOPM said.The organisation called for an urgent, independent and transparent investigation into the allegations.The case has also renewed attention on the vulnerability of Hindu families in Sindh, which has Pakistan's largest Hindu population. VOPM said the problem is particularly acute in rural areas, where poverty, caste discrimination and limited access to legal assistance can leave minority families vulnerable.“This case has caused deep anxiety among Hindu communities in Sindh. Sindh hosts Pakistan’s largest Hindu population, particularly in rural districts where many Hindu families face poverty, caste discrimination and weak access to legal help,” it said.Rights groups have for years raised concerns over allegations involving the abduction, conversion and marriage of minority girls in Pakistan.VOPM cited data from the Centre for Social Justice, included in UK government material, which recorded 421 such cases involving minority girls and women between 2021 and 2024. Hindu women and girls accounted for 282 of those cases, while 72 per cent were reported from Sindh.The organisation said Pakistani authorities recorded at least 83 cases in 2024 alone, with Hindu girls making up 63 per cent of the victims.The concern extends beyond the figures. VOPM also referred to warnings by UN experts in 2026 that nearly 80 per cent of reported cases involving alleged forced conversion through marriage in Pakistan during 2025 took place in Sindh. About 75 per cent of the victims were reportedly Hindus.For VOPM, the immediate focus remains on the two sisters and whether they can speak freely about what happened to them.“Roopi and Seeta’s reported call to return home demands attention. Their protection, age, dignity, and freedom must come before every other consideration,” the VOPM noted.
Article Summary: Roopi, 13 and Seeta, 14, allegedly taken from Ibrahim Colony in Tando Allahyar district. They were allegedly converted to Islam and married to two Muslim men. Rights group calls for an independent probe and safeguards for the girls.

Article Title: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa bombing: Pakistan identifies 'Afghan national' among attackers
Article Text:
The blast was reported near the Old Police Lines in Kohat, in northwestern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province.

(With PTI inputs)

Pakistani officials said Saturday that one of the suicide bombers who targeted a Khyber Pakhtunkhwa mosque was an Afghan national.The explosions killed at least 21 people—including 15 police officers offering Friday prayers at the mosque—and injured 103 others, with police personnel making up the majority of the casualties.According to an investigator, in addition to the attacker identified as an Afghan citizen, efforts to identify a second bomber are ongoing. A joint probe team consisting of local police, the counter-terrorism department, the Elite Force, and security forces is currently investigating the attack.During Friday's assault, the bombers drove an explosives-laden vehicle into the mosque before storming nearby police facilities in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa's Kohat district.Pakistani security authorities have repeatedly accused "Afghanistan-based militant groups" of threatening regional security through terrorism and cross-border infiltration. Islamabad has further accused the Afghan Taliban of harbouring elements linked to the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP)—allegations the Afghan Taliban denies.The Khyber Pakhtunkhwa attack was claimed by Ittehad-ul-Mujahideen Pakistan, a little-known alliance formed last April that includes the Hafiz Gul Bahadur Group, Harakat Inqilab-e-Islami Pakistan, and Lashkar-e-Islam.
Article Summary: One of the suicide bombers who targeted a Khyber Pakhtunkhwa mosque was an Afghan national. The explosions killed at least 21 people, including 15 police officers offering Friday prayers at the mosque. The attack was claimed by Ittehad-ul-Mujahideen Pakistan, a little-known alliance formed last April.

Article Title: Pakistan third from bottom in WEF gender gap index; women lag in workforce
Article Text:
Pakistan's women still behind in workforce

Women remain far behind men in workforce

Education drives improvement

Political representation remains low

Legal rights show gaps

NEW DELHI: Pakistan has ranked 143rd among 145 economies in the World Economic Forum’s (WEF) Global Gender Gap Report 2026, placing it third from the bottom with 59.5% of its gender gap closed. Its score improved by 2.8 percentage points from 2025, marking the country's strongest year-on-year improvement in a decade, according to the report.The WEF index measures gender parity across four areas — economic participation and opportunity, educational attainment, health and survival, and political empowerment, media outlet Dawn cited.Pakistan's overall score has risen by 5.2 percentage points since 2006, when it stood at 54.3%. The WEF said the latest improvement was driven largely by gains in educational attainment.Economic participation continued to be Pakistan's weakest area, with the country scoring 36.4% and ranking 144th globally. Labour-force participation stood at 34.6% parity, while women accounted for 6.5% of legislators, senior officials and managers and 44.9% of professional and technical workers.Parity in estimated earned income stood at 26.3%. The report also found that the share of women in senior leadership and business ownership remained limited.Pakistan recorded a significant improvement in educational attainment, reaching a parity score of 91.7%, more than six percentage points higher than in the previous edition.The WEF said parity in education has improved by 21 percentage points since 2006. Gains were recorded across primary, secondary and tertiary enrolment, making education the main driver of Pakistan's overall improvement in the 2026 index.Pakistan scored 14.1% in political empowerment, ranking 107th globally. While parity in parliamentary and ministerial representation improved from the previous edition, women remained underrepresented in both areas.The report said women accounted for 21.69% of parliamentarians, while men made up 78.31%. Women held just 3.45% of ministerial positions, compared with 96.55% for men.Pakistan also received a score reflecting the period in which a woman has served as head of state, with the report noting that a female head of state had ruled the country for 4.73 of the previous 50 years.The report's contextual indicators also highlighted disparities in women's legal and economic rights. It found unequal rights relating to inheritance for widows and daughters and restricted rights in access to justice. Women were assessed as having near-equal rights regarding access to financial services and assets, while their rights relating to divorce and reproductive autonomy remained restricted.The report also recorded that 24.9% of women had experienced gender-based violence during their lives.
Article Summary: Pakistan ranked 143rd among 145 economies in the World Economic Forum’s (WEF) Global Gender Gap Report 2026. Pakistan's overall score has risen by 5.2 percentage points since 2006, when it stood at 54.3%. The WEF said the latest improvement was driven largely by gains in educational attainment.

Article Title: 'Can't afford petrol': Pakistan PTI lawmakers ride donkey carts to assembly in protest
Article Text:
(Image credit: Dawn) “The ministers and (treasury) MPAs should also reach the assembly the same way on donkey carts,” PTI MPA Sajjad Ali was seen saying in a video while holding a placard describing the fuel price hike as a “petrol bomb dropped on the people”.

Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) workers and provincial lawmakers staged a protest in the Sindh province against soaring fuel prices. They arrived at the provincial assembly by riding donkey carts, saying petrol had become too expensive for them to travel in their vehicles.According to Dawn news, the protest was held after petrol prices rose to Rs 390.79 per litre and high-speed diesel (HSD) to Rs 424.92 per litre following the latest adjustment on Thursday. PTI MPA Sajjad Ali and other lawmakers rode donkey carts from areas near the assembly to its main gate, carrying placards and raising slogans against the federal government.“The ministers and (treasury) MPAs should also reach the assembly the same way on donkey carts,” Ali was seen saying in a video while holding a placard describing the fuel price hike as a “petrol bomb dropped on the people”.Ali said the protest was intended to highlight the difficulties faced by ordinary people because of rising fuel costs.“Petrol has become so expensive that we cannot even come to the assembly in our vehicles,” he said, adding that people were bearing the brunt of the government’s policies.The latest increase comes amid renewed hostilities in the Middle East, which have disrupted major oil supply routes and pushed fuel prices higher over the past two months.The current petrol and diesel prices include government taxes and duties of Rs114 per litre on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel. The government now adjusts fuel prices daily.The Pakistan bar council also criticised the repeated fuel price increases.
